EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:51:27 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 [EXCLUSIVE] Leaked WhatsApps between ex-EU commissioner Reynders and senior Belgian spy reveal attempts to bury allegations of his possible Russia ties https://euobserver.com/243287/exclusive-leaked-whatsapps-between-ex-eu-commissioner-reynders-and-senior-belgian-spy-reveal-attempts-to-bury-allegations-of-his-possible-russia-ties/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243287 The messages, seen by EUobserver and published here in full, now form evidence in a Belgian police investigation into Reynders on money-laundering charges, which paints them in a potentially criminal light.]]> “The ‘job’ … has been mostly accomplished,” said a senior official in Belgium’s spy service, Hugues Brulin, in a WhatsApp message to the Belgian then EU commissioner, Didier Reynders.

“Bravo for the work you did,” said Reynders.

It was back in 2022, and, at least on the surface, they were chatting about a staff reshuffle inside Belgium’s intelligence service, La Sûreté de l’Etat/Veiligheid van de Staat (VSSE) — which was already a peculiar thing for Brulin to be doing on WhatsApp with an EU official.

But their messages, seen by EUobserver and published in full below, were now also evidence in a Belgian police investigation into Reynders on money-laundering charges, which paint them in the light of a potentially criminal conspiracy.

They reconfirmed that Belgian authorities were looking into wider allegations of Reynders’ possible collusion with Russia.

Brulin’s real “job” had been to stop the VSSE from probing Reynders and his potential Russia links, according to five former and current Belgian intelligence officers who spoke to EUobserver.

And Brulin also WhatsApp-ed Reynders on how to “counterattack” a Russia whistleblower.

The 68-year-old liberal politician from Liège, in French-speaking southern Belgium, had had a glittering career before his sudden fall from grace in December 2024, when Belgian police raided his properties, and before he was subsequently charged in 2025 with having laundered some €1m via the ING Bank, using lottery tickets and cash deposits.

Reynders had been EU justice commissioner from 2019 until 30 November 2024 (just four days before the police raid) and Belgium’s foreign and defence minister from 2011 to 2019.

And Belgium had vetted and cleared him to read “top secret” national, EU, and Nato documents.

Meanwhile, Europe was scandalised to learn, on 10 October, that Germany’s former spy chief had been arrested for selling secrets.

But if a figure with Reynders’ CV was also found guilty of corruption and foreign collusion, it would be yet another security fiasco for Western allies.

]]> The EU media connects Europe’s connectors – allow us to help https://euobserver.com/244439/media-connects-europes-connectors/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244439 Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. In doing so, they can help connect the communities that make the European project work. This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community.]]> Europe is a work in progress. Its future depends on the ability of people, institutions and businesses to work together across national borders and political divides.

The European project is far from perfect, but it remains the strongest alternative to a continent defined by division and confrontation.

Europe has advanced through dialogue, negotiation and compromise. Challenging established ideas is part of that process. So is recognising that criticism alone cannot deliver change. The task is to improve what we have built and find common ground on what comes next.

That responsibility extends well beyond the EU institutions and the Brussels bubble.

Businesses, civil society, universities, national governments, media and citizens all have a stake in Europe’s future. The single market and the euro, for example, are not merely institutional achievements. They are also the products of economic cooperation and the participation of businesses and citizens across the continent.

Strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and prosperity should be understood in the same way: as a shared undertaking, not an agenda reserved for political and economic elites. A stronger Europe requires participation, initiative and a willingness to contribute. It cannot be built by those who remain on the sidelines.

Europe needs more Connectors

Construction usually brings to mind roads, bridges and buildings — the concrete structures that link cities, countries and communities. But Europe also relies on less visible infrastructure: the networks, institutions and platforms that bring people together, build trust and turn ideas into action.

Media, civic organisations, universities and professional networks all play a role in this process. They connect perspectives, create opportunities for dialogue and help people identify shared interests across sectors and borders. They make cooperation possible where distance, competing priorities or a lack of understanding might otherwise stand in the way.

These Connectors are essential to Europe’s ability to act collectively. They help businesses engage with policymakers, give citizens access to informed public debate and enable organisations to exchange knowledge and develop partnerships. Their value lies not only in the connections they create, but also in what those connections make possible.

Pan-European media has a particular role to play. Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. In doing so, they can help connect the communities that make the European project work.

This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community. The aim is to create opportunities for organisations to communicate their priorities, strengthen their visibility and engage with the people and ideas shaping Europe’s economic future.

But the ambition goes beyond communication. It is about building relationships between businesses and the wider European ecosystem, encouraging the exchange of ideas and helping organisations find common ground around shared challenges and opportunities.

A competitive and prosperous Europe needs more than sound policies and strong institutions. It needs people and organisations willing to connect, cooperate and contribute. Media can help bring them together.

Europe is still under construction. Let’s connect its Connectors

To explore how we can connect your organisation with the people and ideas shaping Europe, contact us at connector@euobserver.com. 

]]> EU’s Arctic oil-and-gas pledge leaves a Norway-sized loophole https://euobserver.com/244472/eus-arctic-oil-and-gas-pledge-leaves-a-norway-sized-loophole/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244472 If there is no offtake market in continental Europe, no-ne is going to take the risk. The thing is, EU buyers already buy plenty of gas (and oil) from the Arctic.]]> Earlier this week, EU officials said in unusually staunch terms that they would not buy Arctic oil and gas.

Even if someone (Norway) decided to drill new oil or gas wells in the Barents Sea, which is well above the Arctic Circle, the EU would not purchase it.

The goal is to dissuade investors. It costs many billions of euros to develop gas or oil at scale in the harsh conditions of the far north.

If there is no offtake market in continental Europe, no-one is going to take the risk.

Read more

EU vows to stop buying Arctic oil and gas, but drops ban from its new strategy

The thing is, EU buyers already buy gas (and oil) from the Arctic. A lot of it.

Most of the gas, some 12 million tonnes so far this year, comes from Russia’s Yamal LNG plant, which sits on the shore of the biggest estuary you have never heard of, the Gulf of Ob (Obskaya Guba in Russian).

But that will end 10 weeks from now, when the EU ban on Russian LNG kicks in.

]]> EU Parliament defies frugal capitals by seeking €7bn more for the EU’s popular Erasmus+ student scheme https://euobserver.com/244456/meps-defy-frugal-capitals-by-seeking-e7bn-more-for-the-eus-popular-erasmus-student-scheme/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:45:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244456 The parliament overwhelmingly supported an increased budget and scope for the Erasmus+ programme under the new EU budget on Thursday.]]> The European Parliament overwhelmingly supported an increased budget and scope for the Erasmus+ student-exchange programme under the new EU budget on Thursday (22 October).

The plenary in Strasbourg opted for a €7bn increase in Erasmus+’s budget compared to the commission’s proposal, by 454 votes, with 34 abstentions, against 93, mostly from right-wing parties.

And it was an audacious move, seeing as ‘frugal’ EU capitals are pushing for €150bn of cuts to the commission’s draft.

But even a “slight increase” in Erasmus+ funds would mean more opportunities for thousands of people, said Bogdan Zdrojewski, a Polish centre-right MEP, who was the rapporteur on the file, during a parliamentary debate earlier on Wednesday.

Celebrating its 40th anniversary in 2027, Erasmus+ enables young people to study, live, and work in foreign countries both inside the 27 EU states and the programme’s 160 “associate” states worldwide.

Some 17 million people have taken part since it began, with an estimated 1 million babies also born to couples who met on exchange, in what the commission has long used as a flagship PR project for creating a feel-good factor about the EU.

Read more

Leaders eye deep EU budget cuts, while long-term joint borrowing becomes the new normal

Meanwhile, the UK will rejoin the programme in 2027, which means EU students will once more have the opportunity to also spend a semester in Britain, which host some of Europe and the world’s top universities.

And the parliament would also welcome Canada’s full participation in a few years’ time, Zdrojewski told press on Wednesday.

The EU Parliament would like to expand Erasmus+ to more vocational training. “Erasmus+ will be a programme for Europeans no matter what age, what stage of life,” Zdrojewski said.

And students from poorer homes should get more support to live in pricey cities abroad, he added.

The share of Erasmus+ participants who had fewer opportunities to travel under the present structure stood at 15 percent in 2023 – up from 10 percent only two years earlier, according to a commission evaluation.

Read more

MEPs resist 17% cut to EU foreign aid, instead seek €25bn top‑up

“Far too often, it is still the parents’ financial situation that determines who can take part in Erasmus+ and who cannot,” said Sabrina Repp, a German socialist MEP, in Wednesday’s debate in Strasbourg.

Working students often cannot afford to quit their current job to go abroad, she added: “That is precisely what we must change.”

The EU budget talks are to be finalised early next year.

Some 83 percent of Erasmus+ participants say they gained professional skills that helped them in the labour market.

But in order for those opportunities to be available more widely, “we need more funding for this programme,” also said Lucia Yar, a Slovak liberal MEP in the Strasbourg debate.

]]> Drones buzz overhead and enemy wi-fi everywhere: Ukrainian veterans describe how they survived in Russia’s ‘kill zone’ (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,701) https://euobserver.com/244400/drones-buzz-overhead-and-enemy-wi-fi-everywhere-ukrainian-veterans-describe-how-they-survived-in-russias-kill-zone-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1701/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:38:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244400 The kill zone’s constant drone buzz, mined roads and invisible Russian networks are making basic things, such as a phone call, into life-or-death gambles for exhausted Ukrainian troops.]]>
  • Soldiers told the New York Times how they survived six months in the kill zone.
  • Basic rules for survival.
  • Modern warfare: masses of equipment versus courageous individuals.
  • Following peace talks, the humanist Putin sent ballistic missiles to Ukraine.
  • Map of the day: the successful Operation Vivaldi.
  • Videos of the day: the underground Operation Veles into the Russian rear and an aerial drone duel.

    • Soldiers speak about their six months in the kill zone. When the 128th Mechanised Brigade asked at a training ground last autumn who was willing to go into the ‘kill zone’, the term used for the most dangerous stretches of the 1,200-km front, two soldiers volunteered.

    And the rest visibly breathed a sigh of relief.

    Hennadiy and Mykhailo, whose story was reported by the New York Times, spent a long six months “at zero” rather than one, and described in detail how they managed to survive on the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

    Their account shows how, despite drone warfare, the basic work — holding or capturing new positions — is still done by infantry, which remains indispensable even in this war, where a technological advantage can mean the difference between life and death.

    Both set out by car from the village of Prymorske and, when they were about 1.5 km from their destination, began a slow and extremely dangerous journey.

    It was most dangerous when they had to move.

    ]]>         A bigger EU border force Frontex is set to be unveiled with emphasis on deportations https://euobserver.com/244422/a-bigger-eu-border-force-frontex-is-set-to-be-unveiled-with-emphasis-on-deportations/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:24:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244422 The EU's border force Frontex is getting overhauled next Tuesday by a European Commission determined to give the Warsaw-based agency a larger role in deportations, more resources, and more agility to deploy.]]> The EU’s border force Frontex is getting overhauled next Tuesday (27 October) by a European Commission determined to give the Warsaw-based agency a larger role in deportations, more resources, and more agility to deploy.

    The Brussels-executive has already proposed increasing the agency’s budget to €12bn, spread out over seven years. The money is being discussed as part of a larger drawn out EU budget fight among EU states.

    Budget tussles aside, the commission has already dropped clues into what it wants from the new agency, following demands from its political masters at the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP).

    The EPP had wanted to expand the border force to 30,000 from the proposed 10,000. But it is unlikely the 30,000 will be met given the difficulty of finding recruits.

    Frontex currently has around 1,250 officers, who are directly employed by the agency. Its standing corps also includes officers provided by member states on long- and short-term assignments. That means they are not all on the Frontex payroll.

    European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, ahead of this month’s EU summit, instead spoke of a “substantial increase” of the Frontex standing corps, without committing to a number.

    She also called for European Border and Return Reserve, a Quick Reaction Force for crisis deployment, a Return Coordination Centre to accelerate and improve returns including from foreign states, and social media snooping to gauge any possible Ceuta-like mass arrivals.

    The agency is also likely to get more personal data sharing powers with the EU police force Europol.

    ]]>         MEPs back three-year methane delay, triple what the EU Commission wanted https://euobserver.com/244375/meps-back-three-year-methane-delay-triple-what-the-eu-commission-wanted/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 12:25:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244375 The European Parliament has voted to delay EU methane rules for oil and gas importers by three years, two more than the commission proposed. The vote also extends the delay to European producers and opens the door to reopening the law in 2029.]]> The European Parliament on Thursday (22 October) backed a three-year delay to the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas importers, two years more than the European Commission proposed last week.

    MEPs also voted to extend the delay to European oil and gas producers, which goes beyond the commission’s plans.

    The text now forms parliament’s position for negotiations with member states, whose ambassadors failed to agree on Wednesday.

    Under the amendments, tabled by the conservative European People’s Party (EPP), importers would only have to prove that their oil and gas meets EU monitoring standards from 2031, instead of 2027 under the current law.

    Reporting on methane intensity would also be delayed from 2028 to 2031.

    A separate amendment from a cross-party group of 36 Romanian and Bulgarian MEPs, which also passed, delays reporting obligations for EU operators by three years, to 2030.

    MEPs also approved an amendment, tabled by Dutch Socialist MEP Mohammed Chahim, that the extra time should not apply to oil, gas and coal from countries under EU sanctions, which in practice means Russia.

    A far-right Patriots for Europe proposal to suspend the regulation altogether was rejected, as was a push by the conservative ECR group to delay parts of the rules even longer.

    ]]>         International Criminal Court wins EU’s top human rights prize in defiance of Trump’s sanctions https://euobserver.com/244343/international-criminal-court-wins-eus-top-human-rights-prize-in-defiance-of-trumps-sanctions/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 11:24:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244343 The ICC has received the EU’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. The court's president judge thanked lawmakers for the recognition and said "there is no peace without justice and no security without law". ]]> The International Criminal Court (ICC) has received the EU’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.

    Reacting to EU Parliament president Roberta Metsola’s announcement of the prize winner on Thursday (22 October), the Hague-based court said it is “thankful” for the recognition of the court and its officials.

    “This award comes at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges, including sanctions aimed at disrupting the court’s judicial mandate,” ICC president judge Tomoko Akane told EUobserver in a statement.

    The parliament’s recognition “underscores the importance of […] support to enable the Court to carry out its mandate independently and impartially, in the service of justice and the victims of the gravest crimes,” said the Japanese judge.

    The court’s win comes after US president Donald Trump put his weight behind Israeli efforts to discredit the international judicial body by extending sanctions against it.

    The ICC investigates and tries individuals charged with war and human-rights related crimes. When it issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes, the US responded by sanctioning its judges.

    EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the win, saying:
    “For victims of the world’s gravest crimes, justice means a voice. The ICC must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation. Europe stands firmly behind president Tomoko Akane, the Court’s judges and officials, and their vital work for a world governed by rules.”

    Read more

    EU bets on diplomacy, not blocking statute, to protect ICC from Trump sanctions

    New sanctions against the court were announced by the Trump administration this month after the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge who concluded in a UN report that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

    Tomoka said: “While this prize recognises the work of the court in combating impunity and ensuring fair trials, it is also an important recognition of the role of international justice as a cornerstone of lasting peace. In a world marked by rising conflicts, there is no peace without justice and no security without law.”

    Strasbourg stands for justice

    French MEP Chloé Ridel initiated the ICC’s nomination for the Sakharov Prize on behalf of the Socialists & Democrats parliament group.

The only route to escape is tapped with mines and rife with attack drones.]]> A high-ranking EU politician has gone on hunger strike over the humanitarian crisis in besieged Oleshky in Ukraine.

    Pina Picierno, an Italian MEP and a vice-president in the EU parliament, told EUobserver she is refusing to eat solid food to draw attention to the besieged Ukrainian town.

    Eight kilometres from Kherson, Oleshky is reported to now have 1,700 inhabitants, down from 24,000 people before Russia’s full-scale invasion.

    The EU says the town is without access to food, medicine, clean water and basic care.

    The only route to escape is tapped with mines and rife with attack drones, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha warned last Saturday (17 October).

    Saying that Russia wants to make Oleshky a “death trap”, the Ukrainian minister urged the UN and International Red Cross to secure evacuation corridors and immediate humanitarian access to Oleshky.

    “Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails,” he said.

    Pope calls Putin over Oleshky

    The Vatican has attempted to mediate, with Pope Leo calling last week for Russian president Vladimir Putin to arrange a humanitarian ceasefire to allow in aid.

    ]]>         Brussels is moving to ban street advertising by fossil-fuel firms – the EU officials who live there should take note https://euobserver.com/243679/brussels-is-moving-to-ban-street-advertising-by-fossil-fuel-firms-the-eu-officials-who-live-there-should-take-note/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 10:26:59 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243679 Five Brussels municipalities, home to nearly one-in-three of the city's residents, have now voted to drive fossil-fuel advertising off their streets. In the city where Europe's climate laws are written, the industry's grip on billboards and on lawmakers has to be broken together.]]> Last week, Elsene became the fifth  municipality to vote for an end to fossil-fuel advertising, joining Saint-Gilles, Jette, Schaerbeek and Molenbeek.

    Four of those five votes came in the space of just four months, and together, these municipalities are home to roughly 370,000 people: one-third of the Brussels-Capital Region’s population.

    All five are making the same demand: that the Brussels region bans fossil-fuel advertising across the entire city, from metro stations to regional roads. More motions are already being tabled, and by the end of the year, a majority of Brussels’ 19 municipalities could be on record calling for a ban.

    While local politicians are taking the lead, the outlook a little higher up the chain looks less promising. 

    Europe’s ad town and the EU’s lobby town

    Everyday tens of thousands of officials, MEPs, assistants and diplomats brave Brussels morning rush hour on their way to work on the laws that will decide whether Europe meets its climate targets.

    Along the way they pass numerous temptations, bus shelters and metro walls selling them petrol cars, weekend flights and gas contracts, normalising the ongoing mass-consumption of these products. 

    Once they reach their offices, they meet the same industry again, this time in person. The seven biggest oil and gas companies alone have declared lobbying budgets of almost €64m.

    Fossil Free Politics research shows EU Commissioners and their cabinets had nearly 900 meetings with fossil fuel lobbyists in the last term. That’s nearly once every working day, showing just how embedded the industry is in the daily rhythm of Brussels life.

    Some files come under particularly heavy pressure, with one egregious example being how a secretive alliance of eleven large multinational enterprises worked to tear down the EU’s flagship human rights and climate law last year, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD).

    Read more

    MEPs vote in favour of major rollback of corporate sustainability laws

    The fossil fuel industry is currently mounting an extremely intense lobbying campaign to delay and dilute the EU Methane Emissions Regulation over the past year.

    Over 80 percent of all commission meetings with external interest representatives on this regulation involved fossil fuel lobbyists, and the European Parliament is no better. All 17 MEPs who called for the methane regulation to be reopened in an April 2026 letter to the commission had met with fossil fuel lobbyists in the preceding year.

    And those are only the declared figures.

    Lobbyists roaming the corridors

    Safe to say, the real total is almost certainly higher. According to new research by Reclaim Finance, on two out of every three days, the fossil-fuel lobbyists present at the European Parliament had no meetings scheduled with MEPs. They roam the corridors and cafés in the building, aiming to bump into the MEPs they wish to influence.

    The councillors behind these fossil ad ban motions are not pretending that a few billboards will single-handedly solve the climate crisis, but they refuse to continue letting public spaces be misused by the fossil, automotive and aviation industry to freely promote their propaganda; as for the latter, especially since the advertised destinations are often precisely those places that have been the victims of severe climate disruptions..  

    “The summer of 2026 was a painful awakening to the harsh reality of the consequences of the climate crisis,” said Mathias Gyselen, the Ecolo-Groen councillor who tabled Schaerbeek’s motion in September.

    “Heatwaves, heat islands and heat deaths are unfortunately becoming the new normal in the city. Doing nothing is no longer an option.”

    They are right. Advertising is how the fossil fuel industry keeps its social licence, presenting itself as part of the solution while expanding the very products driving the crisis.

    Not just the five sub-municipalities of the Brussels capital acknowledge this, but over 70+ cities worldwide have taken steps to clear their streets from fossil fuel advertising, among them Amsterdam, Sydney, Stockholm and Edinburgh.

    The problems with advertisements, and multi-million euro lobby strategies, are not just that they very much harm the planet, they are also fundamentally undemocratic. 

    Residents, community groups and civil society organisations cannot match the industry’s firepower. They do not have the budgets, the staff or the open doors that put them across the table from lawmakers week after week.

    Europe has dealt with this before.

    ‘Godfathers of climate chaos’

    Tobacco lobbyists no longer get privileged access to health ministers, nor can cigarette brands buy billboards. For many similar reasons the world wants to end fossil fuels, the EU banned tobacco advertising because promoting a deadly product was incompatible with public health.

    UN secretary-general António Guterres made the same comparison in 2024 when he urged every country to ban fossil fuel advertising, naming fossil-fuel companies as the “godfathers of climate chaos”

    Municipal motions are not binding, so the decision now lies with the Brussels-Capital Region, which controls advertising in the metro, along regional roads and on its own infrastructure. A first obvious step is that it should listen to its municipalities and introduce a city-wide ban.

    But the message is also addressed to the institutions on the other side of the Rue de la Loi.

    If the streets of Europe’s capital are being cleared of fossil fuel promotion, the corridors of its institutions should be too. That means limiting the industry’s access to decision-makers, closing the revolving door, and rejecting fossil fuel sponsorship and partnerships, just as the EU did with tobacco.

    The municipalities of Brussels have shown what local democracy looks like. Now it is up to the region and the EU institutions to show that Europe’s capital is not for sale; not on its billboards, and not in its corridors of power.

On Sunday (25 October), a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability after a deadly train station collapse will attempt to do what established opposition forces have repeatedly failed to achieve: translate civic mobilisation into political change.

    The upcoming parliamentary elections are about more than the (re)distribution of seats. They represent the endeavour citizens want and need in a democratic society.

    For several years now, “the students operate according to the principles of direct democracy,” senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, Vasiljević told EUobserver. They gather in “plenums” and make collective decisions.

    The motor behind that movement was anger. The lack of accountability after the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, which killed 16 people was the main trigger.

    Read more

    Why is the EU ignoring Serbia’s student protests?

    Since then, protests have been taken place around in the country. Eventually, they grew into a nationwide challenge to the government. The student movement even marched from Belgrade to Brussels and Strasbourg to appeal to the EU institutions.

    “It brought some irreversible changes that will have a lasting impact on society,” said Vasiljević.

    And these changes could be now transposed into politics. “The country has been held captive for far too long by one ruling party and, in fact, one ruling elite,” Miloje Savić, a volunteering poll observer, told EUobserver.

    For many Serbs, as for Savić, the students’ organisation represent “a tectonic shift in how society is organised and how it should function.”

    The Student List, now the electoral vehicle for the mobilisation, has given people frustrated with established politics a new focus for their demands. The main idea being that political participation can be rebuilt from the ground up.

    “It is not a good time to be living in Serbia. And during my life, I can’t remember a time when it was,” Ivan Bartoš, a 31-year-old organiser of student protests in Bački Petrovac told EUobserver.

    “The institutions have been captured and controlled by the regime. There is not enough institutional space to accommodate these political changes,” Vasiljević said.

    ]]>         Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate https://euobserver.com/243936/europes-youth-asked-for-hope-but-politicians-just-offer-fear-and-hate/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 10:24:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243936 As Europe pours billions into defence and talks up ‘strategic autonomy’, it is quietly undermining its own power by ignoring the students who say they can’t afford the education, housing or stability needed to keep the continent running.]]> Student protests across Europe are a desperate cry for help, an appeal to governments to build a brighter, hope-filled future. Instead of paying attention, European politicians have decided to manhandle the protesters, misrepresent their demands and manipulate public opinion.

    Different narratives are now competing to explain what the protests are really about.

    They want to be taught properly. They want more teachers, an end to overcrowded classes, dilapidated buildings and inadequate school meals and an admissions system that sorts young people by class and postcode.

    In Belgium, students have protested education cuts and fees. Greek students occupied Syntagma Square over rents, student housing and energy bills. Italian students demanded money for schools rather than war.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    But politicians seem intent on telling a different story.

    For many EU leaders it is – yet again – all about migration.

    Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar has decided that the chaos in French cities makes it “clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.”

    Poland’s Donald Tusk, who insists he will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, joined the leaders of Denmark and Italy at the EU leaders’ meeting in Brussels last week to push for an even tougher Fortress Europe.

    Together, they almost succeeded in getting others in the EU to agree to a statement linking crime and “irregular” migration.

    On the other side of the Atlantic, US president Donald Trump instructed Europe to “close your borders and take control, before it is too late!” while his deputy JD Vance criticised Western liberals for bringing the “third world” to France.

    Parts of the media focused on the violence, particularly the looting and destruction carried out by those who have joined the protests to create chaos, rather than on the demands that brought students onto the streets in the first place.

    In France, meanwhile, it was the presidential campaign that shaped the political response, with Marine Le Pen from the National Rally calling for law and order and blaming “decades of immigration” for the violence while her protégé, Jordan Bardella, said the police should have more weapons and greater powers.

    Read more

    Can the EU survive with far-right leaders running major member states? The answer is worrying

    Jean-Luc Mélenchon of France Insoumise, Le Pen’s leading rival in the elections next year, was accused of fuelling student anger. French centrists struggled to find their footing and their voice. President Emmanuel Macron made an angry television appearance before heading to the Middle East with a delegation of business leaders.

    So far, very predictable.

    Old playbook: one enemy, no solution

    Divert, distract, dehumanise and scapegoat are the oldest tricks in wily politicians’ playbook. The well-worn recipe is simple: take a social crisis, remove its economic content, replace it with a face, a religion, a border. Then offer an enemy, not a solution.

    When public services fail, blame the outsider. When wages stagnate, blame the foreigner. When housing becomes impossible, blame the newcomer rather than the landlord, the investor or the government that stopped building.

    And when young people take to the streets, describe them as manipulated, criminal, alien or dangerous. Treat their anger as a threat to public order rather than a warning that something is profoundly wrong. Say there has been foreign manipulation and disinformation.

    Then turn the full force of the state against the symptoms of the crisis while leaving its causes untouched and change the the subject from justice to fear, from schools to borders, from the future to the past.

    Meanwhile, the money goes elsewhere.

    Europe is pouring resources into defence and rearmament. Governments speak endlessly of competitiveness, productivity and strategic autonomy. But these questions cannot become excuses for neglecting the social foundations on which Europe’s future depends.

    Seriously, who is going to make an ageing Europe competitive if the people expected to build its future cannot afford to have one? Who will run Europe’s basic services if migrants go “home”? What does strategic autonomy even mean if young Europeans cannot get a decent education, find secure employment or afford a home?

    Contradictions

    We should know by now that security cannot be measured in weapons alone. It also depends on how secure citizens feel, and whether they believe they have something worth protecting. Security demands that people have politicians they can trust and institutions which work for them.

    A Europe that invests in its military capabilities while allowing its schools, housing systems and public services to deteriorate risks hollowing out its own strength.

    Believe me: I know. I was born in Pakistan, a country which thrives on war and conflict and neglects the well being of its citizens.

    There is another contradiction. As young people struggle to make their voices heard, the EU is planning cuts to funding for civil society organisations that defend rights, support communities, hold power to account and help turn public anger into democratic participation.

    The EU has always – rightly – backed citizens’ calls for democratic participation, equality and inclusion when it happens in Tunisia, Egypt or Hongkong. How can our leaders close down such calls for participation when they are made at home?

    Sadly, politicians and parts of the media have lost young peoples’ trust – and when that faith goes, so does democracy.

    The EU can and must offer young Europeans a story of hope, inclusion and progress towards equality. Leaders who prefer to hallucinate about migrants should spend more time living up to the EU’s values by investing in education, affordable housing, decent jobs and public services.

    We must give our young people a meaningful voice in decisions that will shape their lives. Our collective future quite literally depends on it.

    ]]>         ‘I’m 42 and I’ve spent my entire adult life held captive by Bibi’ – can Israel finally break free of Netanyahu, as Hungary did of Orbán? https://euobserver.com/243796/im-42-and-ive-spent-my-entire-adult-life-held-captive-by-bibi-can-israel-finally-break-free-of-netanyahu-as-hungary-did-of-orban/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 09:15:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243796 Benjamin Netanyahu has not been Israel’s prime minister for every one of those years. Yet even out of office, Israeli politics rarely escaped his gravitational pull. Hungarians know something about that feeling.]]> Over coffee, an Israeli woman I know began to cry. “I’m 42,” she said, “and I’ve spent my entire adult life held captive by Bibi.”

    Benjamin Netanyahu has not been Israel’s prime minister for every one of those years. Yet even out of office, Israeli politics rarely escaped his gravitational pull.

    For him or against him, public life kept arranging itself around his presence.

    Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having previously held office from 1996 to 1999 and from 2009 to 2021, and from 2022 onward.

    Hungarians know something about that feeling. For 16 years, Viktor Orbán was not merely Hungary’s prime minister but the organising fact of Hungarian politics. Institutions bent around him, opponents defined themselves against him, and arguments somehow ended up being about him.

    On 12 April, that era ended.

    Péter Magyar’s insurgent Tisza party defeated Fidesz after 16 uninterrupted years in power. The final results gave Tisza 141 of parliament’s 199 seats, a two-thirds majority.

    The temptation is to tell a simple story of liberation: the dominant leader fell, the spell broke, democracy returned. But political systems leave habits behind, and Orbán’s most durable legacy may prove to be the way Hungarians learned to imagine politics itself.

    That is also Magyar’s dilemma.

    Opposition movements confronting personalised systems often conclude that they, too, need a protagonist capable of gathering diffuse grievances into a political force.

    Yet the qualities that help an insurgency win are not necessarily those needed to build a pluralist order afterwards. Campaigns reward concentration, and democracy depends on dispersing authority.

    A challenger may have to become indispensable in order to win. Governing democratically requires eventually proving that he is not.

    For people my age, Orbán’s rise was a rupture because we remember other governments and possibilities. Many of my students, now in their 20s, do not. Their political adulthood unfolded almost entirely under Fidesz. Orbán was simply there, as unavoidable as the weather.

    Power can come to look distant and durable, participation noble but futile, and institutions captured or irrelevant. Politics becomes something done to you rather than something you do.

    Read more

    Hungary’s conundrum: undoing Orbán – without becoming Orbán 

    Conversations with Orbán

    I know how deeply that can lodge itself in the mind. For five years, I have had countless conversations with Orbán in which I argued with him and tried to persuade him to change course. All of them took place in my dreams.

    Supporters and opponents experienced Orbán’s system differently, but both learned to orient themselves around the same centre of gravity. Loyalists read its signals, while critics watched it constantly and defined themselves against it.

    Parties that spend years confronting a dominant machine tend to centralise themselves. Message discipline becomes existential, disagreement can look like sabotage, and restraint like something to discuss after victory.

    That is why Hungary’s challenge is larger than reversing Orbán’s policies.

    A government elected to repair democratic institutions has to accept restraints precisely when it can most easily avoid them: strengthening parliament even when it dominates it, protecting independent media when they attack the government, and creating institutions whose authority does not depend on proximity to the prime minister.

    Read more

    The Orban-Netanyahu mutual support nexus

    Older Hungarians understandably speak about restoration: rebuilding institutions, restoring judicial independence, returning to democratic normality.

    But “return” means something different when you are 25. You cannot return to a political world you never inhabited. For younger Hungarians, democracy cannot merely be recovered; it has to become real for the first time.

    That distinction matters beyond Hungary. Opponents of personalised populism often offer restoration as their programme.

    Yet generations raised amid democratic erosion may have little memory of the normality they are being asked to recover. Democratic politics has to show that dispersed power need not mean ineffective government, that disagreement need not threaten the state, and that losing an election need not mean losing the country.

    Success should also mean making politics less consuming. Most democratic life is not election night but local meetings, newspapers and arguments about schools, budgets and public space.

    A healthy political order allows citizens to pay less attention to the leader because fewer things depend on what that leader wants. Personalised rule teaches the opposite lesson. Even resistance can become dependence.

    This is where Hungary’s experience returns me to my conversation about Israel.

    Israelis are due to vote on 27 October in an election in which Netanyahu once again occupies much of the political landscape.

    Read more

    No candidate in Israeli election backs a Palestinian state. The EU’s answer is more ‘reforms’, not pressure

    Whatever voters decide, Hungary suggests a question that will remain whenever his long political era eventually ends: can political life be reorganised around institutions and competing interests rather than around the presence, or absence, of one man?

    Removing a dominant political figure does not remove the habits formed around him. Supporters have to imagine their politics without the leader they regarded as indispensable, while opponents have to decide what they stand for when opposition to him is no longer enough to bind them together.

    Hungary’s experience suggests that this is where democratic renewal really begins – not with replacing one dominant figure with another, but with building institutions and political movements that no longer require one.

    My friend’s tears were for the time she felt had been taken from her. Hungary’s younger generation, now free of Orbán, cannot mourn in quite the same way, because many have no memory of political adulthood against which to measure what was lost.

    Their challenge, now, is not to recover an old normal but to create something they have never experienced: a public life in which politics belongs to citizens without consuming them, and in which no leader becomes so indispensable that an entire country must organise itself around him.

      <title>US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-deposition-discovery</link>
      <description><p>Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition</p><p>Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.</p><p>The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-deposition-discovery">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life</link>
      <description><p>New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill</p><p>Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/bp-oil-spill">2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill</a> and has still not fully recovered, according to a new <a href="https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2616554123">study</a>.</p><p>The April 2010<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/jun/05/bp-deepwater-horizon-spill-report-failures-risks"> explosion of an offshore drilling </a>unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/21/french-borrowing-costs-failure-to-pass-budget-govenment-bonds-violent-street-protests</link>
      <description><p>Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests</p><p></p><p>France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.</p><p>With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/21/french-borrowing-costs-failure-to-pass-budget-govenment-bonds-violent-street-protests">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 23 Oct 2026 05:45:18 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Shop Street, Quay Street and more: Who owns Galway’s main thoroughfares?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/shop-street-quay-street-and-more-who-owns-galways-main-thoroughfares/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/shop-street-quay-street-and-more-who-owns-galways-main-thoroughfares/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000For five years, artist Patrick Loewen has used the vacant facade of 47 William Street in Galway as a shop window to sell his small paintings.

“I paint them on the street,” Loewen says. “This is my mercenary work to finance my exhibition coming up in Dawson Street [Dublin] at the end of October.

“I’ve sold to 50 US states from this wall. I’ve got art in Iran, Bahrain, Kuwait as well. None from internet sales, all from the street, and I let everyone pay whatever they can afford so no one’s out of budget.”

The artist from Vancouver, whose studio, People Loves Diamond, is nearby on Dominick Street, has also sold his art on the streets of many cities in North America. He says Galway’s main thoroughfare “is the healthiest street I’ve ever been on”.

“It feels healthier than Dublin, Limerick or Cork too. It’s very friendly. I always say, ‘if you’ve got problems with Galway, you’re looking for them’.”

Nearby on the corner of High Street and Cross Street, stone carver Daithi O’Gorman sells Celtic-designed slates. O’Gorman, who has also done large commissions for local businesses such as Thomas Dillon’s Claddagh Gold, etches many of the slates he sells to tourists on the street.

“Depending on the weather, I could be here three to five days a week.

“I share the street with the buskers, so when I’m finished, the buskers usually come along and ask me, ‘Has anybody asked you for the spot?’ I say no and they take the spot when I finish. So it’s rotation.”

Who owns Galway’s Eyre Square? The billionaires, hoteliers and publicans running the central plaza

Loewen and O’Gorman share Galway’s thoroughfare with more than 100 shops, restaurants and bars trading from the 120 buildings that line Quay Street, High Street, William Street and Williamsgate Street.

Based on a review of planning, company and Tailte Éireann (formerly the Land Registry) records, The Irish Times has established who owns half of the buildings and the results show a large portion of the properties remain in local hands.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

The irony is that it won’t be the racist rhetoric, his role in the Capitol riots, or the self-sabotaging tariffs that remove the Teflon, but something entirely more mundane: gas prices.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.

But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]><![CDATA[Central Bank inquiry made ‘fundamental errors’ in former PTSB chief tracker mortgage case]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:55:20 +0000A tribunal has confirmed that former PTSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against a Central Bank of Ireland inquiry sanctioning him for a role played in the State’s tracker mortgage scandal.

The Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (Ifsat) said that the sole inquiry member, Peter Hinchliffe, made errors of law that were so fundamental that they negated his decision last year that Guinane be fined €80,000 and reprimanded.

The tribunal concluded in a decision published on Thursday that Hinchliffe “erred in law”, acted beyond what was established by case law elsewhere, “failed to give fair notice of certain issues”, and “failed to give reasons for his decision”.

“Moreover, it held that the errors of law in the inquiry decision were manifest from the text and were fundamental so as to deprive the decision of its basis,” said the tribunal, chaired by chaired by former Supreme Court judge John MacMenamin.

Its conclusion still needs to be confirmed by the High Court. The Central Bank said it does not plan to appeal it.

The Irish Times first reported on the conclusion of the appeal last month.

Former PTSB chief wins appeal over tracker mortgage sanction

“This deeply flawed process, which has cost millions in taxpayer funds, has had a profound effect on my family and on my career,” said Guinane in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

“With this now-discredited allegation, the Central Bank tried to single me out as a scapegoat. It is extraordinary that I was the only individual to be subject to a formal inquiry in respect of the tracker issue.”

Ifsat said that the Central Bank should pay Guinane’s legal costs for the inquiry and appeal, including his €5,000 appeal fee.

It rejected an application by PTSB, a notice party in the case, for costs. PTSB paid a €21 million fine in 2019 for its role in the industry-wide tracker mortgage scandal.

Hinchliffe emphasised last year there was “no finding of dishonesty against Mr Guinane” and that he “did not form an intention to harm or take advantage of customers”. Guinane was also entitled to receive better support from within the wider Irish Life & Permanent Group, of which PTSB was a part at the time, he added.

The inquiry centred on a special condition in some PTSB tracker mortgages offered during the pre-crash property boom. This required customers who moved for a period to a fixed rate to instruct the bank afterwards to put them back on a tracker rate or another fixed product. Otherwise, they would default to a standard variable rate.

The ambiguous wording of the condition led to questions in early 2009 about whether a customer opting to go back on to a tracker rate was entitled to their original margin over the European Central Bank rate, or a higher margin then on offer from PTSB.

The bank adopted a strategy in January 2009, on the basis of legal advice, to only put customers who requested the original rate – or complained – on the more favourable rate. The Central Bank said Guinane signed off on the strategy when he responded to the plan, when advanced by a colleague via email in January 2009, with the words, “okay to that”.

Guinane testified during an inquiry hearing in early 2024 that while he did not remember events surrounding the decision, he understood the email to mean – based on having reviewed documents – that “any customer” coming out of the fixed rate would “go back to their original rate”. The email only contained a summary of the legal advice.

The grounds for the Central Bank’s decision to hold the inquiry were that Guinane knew and understood the strategy.

However, Ifsat said Hinchliffe reframed the allegation by removing “those critical elements of knowledge and approval”.

Instead, Hinchliffe criticised Guinane’s “failure” to ask certain questions, to make follow-up enquiries, or to take other steps which might have shown him what was happening to PTSB customers.

“The meaning of the allegation, as originally notified to the appellant was fundamentally altered in the ultimate decision,” Ifsat said.

The Ifsat decision raises questions about whether the Central Bank will still go after other bankers suspected of having played a role in the tracker mortgage scandal.

Ifsat’s conclusion marks another major setback for the regulator’s post-crisis vetting and enforcement activities.

Ifsat was previously highly critical in 2024 of a Central Bank refusal to approve a board nominee for a fund, saying the decision-making process was “flawed” and denied the individual fair procedures “at every stage”.

The Central Bank was also found in a High Court ruling, published in April, to have badly handled an enforcement investigation into a funds industry executive, saying it was “irretrievably tainted” by errors. The bank committed to learning lessons and changing procedures as a result of both cases.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Why did huge swathes of the internet suddenly go offline yesterday?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:49:59 +0000It caught countless website developers off guard and has left many wondering how protected their cyber systems really are.

When the team behind computer programming language PHP, which powers an estimated 70 per cent of all websites, warned on Wednesday that its software contained “critical vulnerabilities”, it sent the internet into a frenzy.

“Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests,” the developers put it bluntly, but not so simply – “all installations serving web requests” means, in layman’s terms, a website that you can click on.

Users were advised to update immediately or take their sites offline to avoid a cyberattack. While the vulnerability was largely contained within 24 hours of being identified, the fright it has caused will not be easily forgotten.

What is PHP?

“It’s essentially a framework that websites run on,” says Martin Potgieter, the chief technology officer for the South African arm of Integrity 360, a Dublin-based cybersecurity consultancy firm.

Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all

While it’s difficult to say just how many websites run on it, estimates hover around 70 per cent. “A large number of websites on the internet are using it,” Potgieter says.

“It’s an open source code, that’s why it’s so extensively used,” he adds. “Many people might say ‘oh, well, it’s an open source code so that’s why it’s insecure’, but that’s not really the case – it doesn’t make it less secure, just more available.”

]]>Gabby Jones<![CDATA[Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:56:00 +0000When I moved here from New York more than three decades ago, I became the default complainer in restaurants. It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”

If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?

As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.

Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.

William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.

“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.

Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicates that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euro in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.

The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.

Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.

Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.

Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.

When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.

Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.

Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.

“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”

Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.

She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.

Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”

Managing conflict: Top tips:

1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;

2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;

3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;

4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;

5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

  • Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

]]><![CDATA[Aviation firm co-founder ousted during sick leave wins €41,000 for unfair dismissal at WRC]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 18:01:19 +0000

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.

*This article was amended on 21st of October to make clear that Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, Gerry Burke, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley and that Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, Magellan Aviation, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors.

Securing a job offer is the first step, as employers often assess visa requirements early in the hiring process, according to Breda Dooley, head of recruitment at Matrix.

The role must have a minimum salary of €36,605, though the salary for meat processors, horticultural workers, healthcare assistants and home carers must be at least €32,691.

Workers on general employment permits must complete 57 months before they are eligible to apply for Stamp 4 permission.
