]]><![CDATA[Netflix sales growth to slow for fourth quarter ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/netflix-sales-growth-to-slow-for-fourth-quarter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/netflix-sales-growth-to-slow-for-fourth-quarter/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 06:31:29 +0000Netflix reported its slowest sales jump in three years and forecast a fourth consecutive quarter of slowing growth, a projection that amplifies concerns about the world’s leading online TV network.

Netflix delivered sales of $12.9 billion (€11.5 billion) in the third quarter, in line with Wall Street’s expectations, and forecast sales of $13.4 billion in the year’s final three months, falling short of what analysts have predicted. The pace of growth has fallen from 17.6 per cent in the final quarter of last year to a projection of 11.5 per cent for this year’s fourth quarter.

The company blamed its sales shortfall on the advertising business, which is on pace to deliver $300 million less than the company expected.

Shares fell as much as 7 per cent in trading after the results were announced.

“I know we can do better,” Netflix co-chief executive Greg Peters said on a call with analysts Tuesday. “That better is our upside.”

Over the past week, Peters and co-CEO Ted Sarandos have overhauled the company’s leadership to address what they see as a decline in programming quality. Netflix fired chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin just days after announcing cuts of 6 per cent of the staff, or about 1,000 people. The last time Netflix made such substantial reductions was in 2022, when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.

The company’s operating margin forecast for the fourth quarter of 26 per cent is impacted by costs associated with the job cuts. Earnings of 87 cents per share in the third quarter exceeded analysts’ projections for 82 cents.

Sarandos and Peters are walking a tightrope, seeking to assure investors that the company has a bright future while acknowledging things aren’t going as well as everyone would like. Netflix remains a clear leader in streaming. It has more than 325 million subscribers, which the company says equates to almost 1 billion viewers. It accounts for more viewing than any other Hollywood streaming service.

But Hollywood studios don’t overhaul their programming teams when everything is hunky dory. Netflix has gone months without a large, culture-shaping hit in film or TV and has struggled to lure viewers to both new shows and new seasons of older shows. Netflix’s haul of Emmy Awards fell to a 10-year low in 2026.

Sarandos and Peters brought in Peter Rice, a veteran film and TV executive who previously served as chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney Co, and before that as president of 21st century Fox, to replace Bajaria.

“We see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the US,” Sarandos said, touting Rice’s experience in all aspects of entertainment. Rice has worked in film and TV as both an executive and a producer. He also has deep relationships with top filmmakers.

“We want Netflix to always be the place people want to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said.

Long a Wall Street darling, Netflix has faced growing scepticism ever since it made a play to buy the streaming and studios businesses of Warner Bros Discovery.

After losing out in its bid, Netflix has struggled to convince investors it has a viable growth strategy. The stock is down about 25 per cent this year and more than 40 per cent from a year ago.

Investors and analysts have pestered Netflix’s leadership about stagnant engagement. Netflix’s share of US TV viewership sits at 7.8 per cent, according to ratings tracker Nielsen, far behind YouTube, which captures about 14 per cent. And Netflix viewers watched only 2 per cent more programming in the first half of the year than a year earlier.

As Netflix has grown from a small US streaming service into a global behemoth, it has evolved from a producer of “prestige TV” shows like House of Cards and The Crown to a broader entertainment platform, competing with everything from sports channels to YouTube influencers.

Bajaria led the division that released hits like Squid Game and Wednesday, and helped shepherd Netflix’s live programming era with sports and an expanded unscripted portfolio.

But Bajaria’s hot touch cooled over the last year, and many began to question the quality of Netflix’s programming.

“Investors will need, in short order, some indications toward confidence in the growth trajectory that this powerful, global platform should be able to provide,” David Joyce, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said in a note before the results were released.

Netflix is seeking to increase the amount of time its users spend on the service by expanding into live sports, podcasts and video games while also integrating film and TV programming from third parties like TF1 in France. Peters said the company is open to integrating programming from other companies and will also look to sell other streaming services within Netflix. -Bloomberg

]]>Hannibal Hanschke<![CDATA[SpaceX and Tesla boards explore potential merger]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/spacex-and-tesla-boards-explore-potential-merger/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/spacex-and-tesla-boards-explore-potential-merger/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 06:29:18 +0000SpaceX and Tesla are studying a deal to unite Elon Musk’s two public companies in a multitrillion-dollar combination that would be the largest merger of all time.

The world’s richest person on Tuesday said both companies had formed special committees to study a tie-up. It marks the biggest step towards a merger that would create a sprawling conglomerate oriented around AI and potentially worth more than $3 trillion (€2.67 trillion.

“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes. But at the end of the day the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” Musk said, adding that as chief executive of both companies he cannot participate in the discussions.

“The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction, and obviously there is no guarantee that they will,” he added.

SpaceX has a market value of $2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $1.5 trillion. On paper, combining the seventh and 11th most valuable companies in the world would vault Amazon and leave the new entity behind only Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple and Nvidia.

The electric-car maker has deepened its ties with SpaceX in recent years. In March, Musk announced a joint venture called Terafab, a large semiconductor manufacturing plant in Texas that will produce chips for his autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots and orbital artificial intelligence (AI) data centres that could ultimately cost $119 billion.

“There is a lot of merit to combining the two companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said.

The two companies have also teamed up to produce a “flying” sports car called Roadster, unveiled last week. It performed a series of inverted backflips and jumps using cold-gas thrusters developed by SpaceX. Musk’s AI model Grok is provided for free in many Tesla vehicles.

“There is a lot to be gained from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab, robotics, mass to orbit with the [Starlink] constellation connectivity,” Musk said. He has previously rolled the social media platform X and his AI lab, xAI, into SpaceX.

Tesla shares rose about 1.5 per cent after hours, while those of SpaceX climbed 8 per cent after it reported strong earnings.

SpaceX said its revenue more than doubled in the third quarter, swinging the company into profit and calming investor nerves about accelerating spending on AI.

Revenue surged 161 per cent to $14.6 billion in the third quarter, up from $5.6 billion a year ago and beating analysts’ estimates of $12.9 billion, the company said.

SpaceX posted a net profit of $4.4 billion in the three months to the end of September, exceeding Wall Street’s expectations of about $2 billion. It made a net loss of $1.1 billion in the same period last year.

The outperformance was driven by sales of cloud computing services, with revenue from AI surging ninefold to $7.6 billion from $813mn a year ago and tripling from $2.56 billion in the previous quarter.

SpaceX continued to spend heavily on AI. Capital expenditure rose to $19.6 billion from $18.4 billion in the prior quarter and more than consensus estimates of $18 billion compiled by Factset.

The vast majority of that investment was on data centres and chips, and Musk said capex would climb again to between $35 billion and $40 billion in the fourth quarter – much more than analysts expected.

Musk has rapidly transformed the company into an AI data centre provider, striking deals to lease its excess computing capacity. Rival model developers, notably Anthropic and Google, have proven willing to pay premium prices to secure access to the chips needed to train and run their models.

Musk said he was being “hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute. We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.”

SpaceX said it had 1.7 gigawatts of installed computing capacity at the end of September. The size of its pair of Colossus data centres now surpasses the 1.5GW of active power that CoreWeave, the largest listed “neocloud”, had online at the end of June.

On a call with investors, Musk said he would be “surprised” if SpaceX did not have 13GW by the end of next year, with a “small, non-zero possibility” that capacity could reach 20GW. That is roughly equivalent to twice the peak power consumption of New York City.

A computer-generated video of SpaceX’s Starship landing back on Earth

Musk’s opportunistic move into renting out data centres has grown into a lucrative business but has led to concerns that SpaceX’s internal AI efforts are failing to gain traction.

The earnings report is the second since the rocket-and-AI group raised $86 billion in the largest initial public offering ever in June at a $2 trillion valuation. The shares initially surged but have tumbled from a peak of $225 in the week after going public to $148 on Tuesday.

Revenue from Starlink, its 11,000-strong network of broadband satellites, rose to $5.2 billion from $3 billion the year before, and it reported net income of $2.4 billion in the quarter.

SpaceX has recently become embroiled in tensions between Ukraine and the Trump administration. Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces have been hit by speed limitations that disrupted the ability to deploy drones, which President Volodymyr Zelenskiy blamed on a “planned operation ... to restrict us”.

SpaceX’s launch business rose to $1.8 billion in revenue, but it made a small loss during the period. Last month, its skyscraper-sized rocket Starship reached orbit for the first time, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites that it says will significantly increase the network’s capacity.

The 400ft rocket is core to Musk’s sci-fi ambitions to build a network of orbital AI data centres, start a lunar economy and colonise Mars. On Tuesday, he said SpaceX would attempt to catch the booster and spacecraft stages with mechanical “Mechazilla” arms during the next test flight in November. -Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445841/">
   <title>Bisher keine Angriffe in Österreich bekannt</title>
   <description>Weltweit hat es Millionen Versuche von Cyberangriffen auf Websites gegeben, nachdem am Mittwoch gravierende Sicherheitslücken in der Programmiersprache PHP bekanntgeworden waren.    <title>Ferienwoche meist trocken und herbstlich</title>
   <description>Typisch für Herbst bringt die kommende Woche sehr unterschiedliches Wetter in Europa. Südspanien bietet noch einen Hauch von Sommer mit 25 Grad und mehr. Der Großteil von Island liegt hingegen bald unter der ersten Schneedecke dieses Herbstes. Klimatologisch gesehen ist in Österreich Ende Oktober prinzipiell beides möglich: ein letztes Aufbäumen des Sommers und Schnee bis ins Flachland.</description>

Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year.

The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself.

▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości.
▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026

Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons.

After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused.

On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then.

Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week.

"Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026

On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway.

The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban.

Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.

 

Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN.

The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”.

Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty.

A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”.

However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026

The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”.

In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations.

Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia.

Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states.

The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.

Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.

During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.

📍 New Delhi | Premier @donaldtusk spotkał się z Premierem Indii @narendramodi. pic.twitter.com/Y9HPLQsvf4

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026

Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.

Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.

“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.

Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”

 

Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.

Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.

“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”

However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals.

The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".

"Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility.

To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.

Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”.

Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said that his country would continue to “press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them”.

🇵🇸 I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, against Palestinians, our Consul General, French and Polish diplomats as well as catholic representatives. A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team…

— Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 17, 2026

In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu had urged people to show “caution before drawing conclusions” over what had happened. He claimed that there is “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents” of the West Bank.

However, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said that it “strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters”. But it added that “the consulate’s visit was not coordinated with the IDF”, which is “important to prevent incidents of this kind”.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, also issued a condemnation of the attack and said that police had opened an investigation.

The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.

Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by…

— Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026

The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured.

Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”.

That incident prompted criticism of Israel from the United States, whose ambassador, Mike Huckabee, called it a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”.

.@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK

— CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026

In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból.

In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza.

Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. The Israeli foreign ministry called the remarks “unacceptable” and urged Tusk to “remember the lessons” of the Holocaust.

    Sport’s hiking of ticket prices for live sport is completely at odds with many of its marketing efforts and risks alienating future generations of would-be fans, writes Matt Readman.     Sport’s hiking of ticket prices for live sport is completely at odds with many of its marketing efforts and risks alienating future generations of would-be fans, writes Matt Readman.

    Last week, a BBC Sport investigation revealed just how sharply the cost of watching live sport has risen in the UK. Across the Ashes, the Open, Wimbledon, Formula 1, the Ryder Cup and FA Cup, selected ticket prices have increased by an average of around 90 per cent in just a few years – more than twice the rate of inflation.

    Sports executives have rallied to defend this. Operating costs have risen. So too have fan expectations. And, they argue, the profits flow back into grassroots sport. All fair points. But let’s be honest about the underlying reason: they’re raising prices because they can.

    Like any market, ticket prices are governed by supply and demand. And the UK is fortunate that its biggest sporting events have never been more desirable. Sports executives will argue that their prices are justifiably in line with market value. But this is circular logic. 

    Nobody wants to be the one leaving money on the table, but the worry is that live sport’s ticketing market begins to spiral out of control. Keep increasing prices at this rate and we won’t simply change what fans pay, we’ll change what fans we have altogether. 

    There’s a famous line from Jeff Goldblum’s character in Jurassic Park: “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.” It’s a question sport needs to ask itself: not whether it can charge these prices, but whether it should.

    We want to get kids off screens but price them out of alternatives

    The first consideration is a moral one. Should sporting institutions take advantage of the very people who sustain them? Fans’ loyalty is valuable. But it also makes them vulnerable.

    The second reflection is political. A recent DCMS report found that adults living in the most deprived parts of the country were only half as likely to attend live sport as those in the least deprived. 

    Sport is part of our national culture. Yet the more expensive it becomes, the more exclusive it gets. If only affluent families can afford to attend major events, we risk cutting entire communities off from the sports that have traditionally brought people together. 

    Sport also needs to be careful it doesn’t sacrifice its long-term commercial health for short-term gains. We know that fandom takes root much earlier than many people realise. Yet ticket prices increasingly prevent young people from experiencing live sport in the way previous generations did.

    There are attempts to address this. The Open, for example, offers free tickets to under-16s. That’s a generous offer in principle, but when an adult ticket costs more than £150 it’s hardly an accessible family day out. And it’s an example that many arenas, where every seat is a valuable commodity, would struggle to follow.

    Meanwhile, a 2026 Youth Sport Trust report found that 77 per cent of parents believe screen use is reducing the time children spend being physically active. We’re desperately trying to get children off screens and into the real world. Yet when it comes to live sport, we’re actively doing the opposite.

    Sport is turning its biggest occasions into playgrounds for the privileged

    Perhaps the biggest frustration for me as a marketer is the contradiction in how these sports brand themselves. 

    Over the past decade I’ve worked on countless briefs, across tennis, golf, cricket and rugby, where the challenge is almost always the same: modernise the brand, become more progressive, more accessible and attract more diverse audiences. In other words, we want to shake off the image that we’re narrow and exclusive.

    But what kind of audience does the Ryder Cup in Ireland expect to attract when tickets cost £430? It won’t be the local kids who might become the next Shane Lowry or Rory McIlroy. It will only reinforce the same stereotypes that sports marketers are being paid to dismantle.

    The irony is that ticket sales often represent only a fraction of the overall revenue generated by major sporting events. Yet in the pursuit of maximising every last pound from a finite number of tickets, we risk turning our biggest sporting occasions into playgrounds for the privileged.

    And that’s the real danger. Not simply that fans are being priced out today, but that the next generation may never feel these places are meant for them in the first place.

    Chancellor John Healey has said a package to streamline regulation on reporting requirements as well as further tariff reductions will save businesses around £800m a year.  In a pre-Budget announcement to offer “breathing space” to businesses, Healey confirmed that the government would make reporting requirements for firms and asset managers easier.  The changes on reporting [...]]]>

    Chancellor John Healey has said a package to streamline regulation on reporting requirements as well as further tariff reductions will save businesses around £800m a year. 

    In a pre-Budget announcement to offer “breathing space” to businesses, Healey confirmed that the government would make reporting requirements for firms and asset managers easier. 

    The changes on reporting regulations and an extension of import tariff suspensions on more than 250 products contribute towards a government target to reduce the administrative burden of regulation by 25 per cent by 2030. 

    “British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses,” Healey said.

    “That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

    Andy Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds will convene business leaders in Number 10 North on Friday to discuss reforms. The Labour government has pushed to implement a ‘Tell Us Once’ principle on reporting requirements. 

    The government said compliance rules would become easier for business owners while a simplification of corporate reporting requirements could save businesses operating as part of a wider group about £20,000 a year. 

    Small businesses will not have to file profit and losses on Companies House, a public database for firms’ accounts, for April 2028.

    Healey backs ‘bloody-minded’ businesses

    The new policies follow the creation of a ‘small business regulatory taskforce’ featuring top industry group leaders and government officials to cut costs for businesses. 

    Tina McKenzie, the chair Federation of Small Businesses, who was also a part of the group, said new plans would “help lessen the burden of red tape on small businesses, enabling them to devote more resources to growth and job creation”. 

    Burnham said it was “not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street”. 

    Healey has taken steps to woo businesses ahead of the Budget, even as some economists believe his headroom has been halved to around £12bn and expectations that he may need to raise taxes in order to ease pressures on public finances.

    He pledged to back “bloody-minded” business founders looking to make a profit. 

    “I want to be a Chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit and those entrepreneurs who, in the end, are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying – some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness – to keep going through these sorts of pressures,” he told The Times.

    Andy Burnham wants to undo Brexit because he’s given on the supply side reforms Britain needs for growth, says Joseph Dinnage

    October is always grim. The temperature drops, the rain begins and the darkness sets in. This month is poised to be even drearier than usual. In a week’s time, we’ll have John Healey’s first Budget. 

    Healey will struggle to make up the difference. Cue  tax rises. Expected announcements include higher taxes on banks, online retailers and a fuel duty hike. The government has given up on a domestic growth strategy. Supply-side reform and trimming the state are nowhere to be seen. Perhaps that explains its infatuation with the European Union.  

    It came as no shock to anyone when in his keynote address at the annual Labour Party conference, Andy Burnham set out his plan for closer relations with the bloc.  

    The Prime Minister asserted that we need to move past the Brexit ‘status quo’ and seriously reexamine our place in Europe to stimulate economic growth.  

    How disingenuous. As we saw with the ill-fated Welfare Bill, the truth is that the Prime Minister is throwing in his lot with the EU because his MPs are incapable of voting for the necessary domestic policies which would boost British prosperity. What we will get instead under the government’s EU ‘reset’ is a regulator’s charter that will set us back in the progress we have made in developing the industries of the future. Hugging Brussels closer is probably the one thing Burnham can get most of his MPs to agree upon.  

    Brexit is an AI opportunity

    Despite the previous government failing to diverge from EU orthodoxy as much as one might hope, being independent of the EU has come with a host of opportunities. One of the great benefits of Brexit has been our ability to push ahead with a sensible, independent regime for artificial intelligence outside the EU. Britain’s AI sector is currently much more agile and start-up-friendly than Europe’s, largely due to the EU AI Act, a top-down diktat which has stifled native innovation. It is no wonder that Britain’s AI businesses attracted more investment in the last six months than the entirety of the EU’s AI economy in the same time.

    Our small businesses would feel the pain of rejoining the EU acutely. The EU’s regulations on packaging are putting up trade barriers within Europe rather than bringing them down, making it unviable for SMEs to sell across the continent, and new green regulations like ETS 2 are adding carbon taxes to road transport and construction. Why add taxes like that onto our economy at a time of growing inflation? 

    The warning signs for Britain’s future if we were to rejoin are everywhere. Just look at France and Germany. The bloc’s two major players both face high energy costs, sluggish growth, low productivity and ageing populations. Sound familiar? It is illogical to suggest that by reshackling ourselves to Brussels, our problems would somehow disappear. It certainly has not been the case for some of the Continent’s largest economies, so why would it be any different for us? Besides, outside of the EU we at least have the opportunity to implement policies that would improve our lot. Not that this Government shows any signs of taking it. 

    Of course, there is also the small matter of democracy. Just because Burnham thinks leaving the EU was the wrong decision does not entitle him to overturn the democratic will of millions of voters. 

    Britain needs growth. Burnham knows it. Healey knows it. We all know it. Rejoining the EU would be retrograde and undemocratic act of economic self-harm. It would be no replacement for pursuing policies here at home which – while flying in the face of Labour’s worst instincts – would improve life for all of us. It will take courage, but the government must act in the national interest, not that of its socialist backbenchers.  

    ]]>     2467963Joseph Dinnage Joseph Dinnage     Business needs to speak up in Britain’s battle of ideas https://www.cityam.com/business-needs-to-speak-up-in-britains-battle-of-ideas/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:29:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2468218

    Politics is about to get more stark and much more consequential. Business leaders need to be pragmatic, dealing with the government of the day. But it strikes me that in this battle of ideas, they need to stand up for what works – especially when the country we all love is going in the wrong direction, [...]]]>

    Politics is about to get more stark and much more consequential. Business leaders need to be pragmatic, dealing with the government of the day. But it strikes me that in this battle of ideas, they need to stand up for what works – especially when the country we all love is going in the wrong direction, says Liam Halligan

    Earlier this week, I was delighted to address a Confederation of British Industry reception at the British Museum – with a chance to see the magnificent Bayeux Tapestry depicting, of course, the Battle of Hastings.

    While 1066 was a long time ago, there’s another battle going on now, across our politics and the economy – a Battle of Ideas.

    Britain remains a great place to live and work – boasting enormous scientific and artistic acumen.

    And – crucially – we’re home to some great businesses, small and large, run by talented, driven entrepreneurs.

    But for quite a few years now, commercial success achieved in Britain has been despite rather than because of government policies.

    For decades, under the Tories and now Labour, the state has been getting bigger – and is now far too intrusive and chronically unaffordable, to the extent it’s threatening financial stability.

    After the big government of the 1970s, the tax burden fell steadily to 30 per cent of GDP by the early 1990s, the end of the Thatcher era.

    It rose again under New Labour and pretty steadily during 14 years of Tory-led government.

    Over the last two years, though, since Labour regained office, Britain’s tax burden has spiralled. From 38 per cent now – the highest since 1948 – we’re heading for 41 per cent by the end of this decade. And that’s before next week’s budget.

    Increasingly, the centre-left wants yet higher taxes, more state borrowing and spending – bigger government. The centre-right is meanwhile pushing for lower taxes, government that does less, a smaller state.

    Business leaders need to be pragmatic

    This is the battle of ideas now looming over the British economy. That’s why politics is about to get more stark and much more consequential.

    Business leaders need to be pragmatic, dealing with the government of the day. But it strikes me that in this battle of ideas, they need to stand up for what works – especially when the country we all love is going in the wrong direction.

    When you look at our high inflation, spiralling energy costs, rising unemployment and, particularly, our increasingly precarious public finances, Britain clearly is (italics) going in the wrong direction.

    For years, we’ve lived beyond our means – with governments of all stripes racking up huge borrowing and debts.

    The government borrowed £24.5bn last month – almost £11bn of which was spent on debt interest payments, £400 per household on debt service costs, in September alone.

    Debt interest payments since April amount to £61bn – that’s our annual defence budget, enough to build 40 brand new hospitals, or employ 100 thousand extra nurses for ten years.

    This isn’t how you’d run a business and it’s now how we should be running our country.

    Unlike Hastings, this isn’t a battle with France. But ministers often tell me our friends across the channel have a higher national debt than we do. Yes, but Britain’s debt has been growing so far, and we’ve become so inflation prone, we pay far more to borrow – with annual debt service costs now 3.6pc of GDP, compared to 2.5pc in France.

    The UK’s public finances are dangerously fragile and could easily implode. Former senior officials at the Bank of England and Office of Budget Responsibility are now speaking out. Business leaders need to speak out too.

    A battle of ideas is looming, with Britain at a fork in the economic policy road. Not quite as consequential as the Norman Invasion, it will nonetheless significantly impact the lives and livelihoods of millions of British households.

    Prima Facie review and star rating: ★★★★

    In London, only 3 per cent of reported rapes lead to a suspect being charged. It is a fact so shocking that even people with no interest in the courts recite it. It is the problem that forms the backdrop of Suzie Miller’s very good 2022 play of the same name as this film, which starred Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer, who in a 100 minutes of theatre astonishingly played every character from the court judge to the victim. 

    Miller’s writing, for which she won the Olivier Award in 2023, extracts a compelling human story out of this institutional crisis. Prima Facie follows Tessa Ensler, a successful criminal defence barrister who has become rich protecting men who are probably guilty of crimes by finding legal loopholes. But an incident in her personal life forces her to rethink the morality of her work. 

    Prima Facie: film can be didactic

    Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo takes over from Comer for Susanna White’s screen adaptation, alongside a supporting cast (Erivo played dozens of characters was presumably harder to land on film). Still, a similar sense of horror is conjured. As Ensler, Erivo brings the sort of muscular fortitude that demonstrates how this young working class woman would graduate to this kind of job that’s typically reserved for the private schooled elite. She is also brilliant at conveying Ensler’s vulnerability; as she experiences a personal breakdown, Erivo’s angular, cocksure barrister softens, her eyes becoming wide chasms of overwhelm.

    There’s an attempt to retain the character-driven intensity of the stage production, via a wealth of tracking shots of Erivo walking past London courthouses and along the river while the camera lingers close. It’s straightforwardly shot and rarely distracted by bells and whistles.

    Harrowing plot

    There have been complaints of didacticness, and at a few points, I am taken briefly out of the action when a line or two is too on-the-nose, moralising about the ways the legal system needs to change. But I’d argue that some of this is inevitable. The story is set in a courtroom, the literal bedrock for conversations about ways to change the world. The one place where you do get to stand up and have your say. Perhaps Prima Facie has an excuse to tell us how to feel more than most. 

    It’s certainly a minor distraction from a terrific depiction of the injustices so many women face, and a truly harrowing plot – multiple women ran out in tears during the London Film Festival screening, and this male critic joined them in weeping throughout. Like the West End show, this Prima Facie finds a compelling and totally shocking human story amid a legal system that seems to have forgotten about the victims. 

    Prima Facie is in UK cinemas on 13 November 2026

    Investing in a football stadium can be the difference between sinking and swimming and the government must play a role, writes Joseph Smith.

    It is fair to say that the Independent Football Regulator’s draft State of the Game report provides the most comprehensive analysis of English football’s finances to date. Published last week and open for consultation until the end of the year, it highlights that while English football is both highly competitive and wealthy it faces significant financial risk.

    The report’s key findings? That 94 per cent of clubs in the top five divisions – from the Premier League down to the National League – operated at a loss, and that two thirds could not survive 90 days without additional funding from existing owners. Nearly 20 EFL and National League clubs reported non-player operating cost figures that were higher than their total revenues.

    The regulator was established because parliament determined that football clubs are not ordinary businesses. Since a club cannot be easily replaced if it fails, the Football Governance Act imposes a level of scrutiny uncommon in most industries.

    The long-standing debate

    Debate has long focused on television revenue – which for the Premier League is into the billions – including redistribution and parachute payments from the top flight. However, the regulator highlights that matchday income becomes increasingly important further down the league pyramid. In the top division it represented 14 per cent of revenue but that rises to 19 per cent in the Championship and 35 per cent in Leagues One and Two.

    Matchday income is therefore essential, and stadium improvements can be a direct way to achieve this. Larger stadiums allow for more ticket sales where demand exists, and enhanced facilities support higher-value matchday and commercial activities – tiers of premium seating have been a popular addition to many stadiums over the last decade. The regulator concludes that investment in stadiums and infrastructure has significantly increased revenue for the largest clubs.

    Premier League clubs benefit from higher ticket prices, stronger demand and corporate hospitality, and invested £2.2bn in infrastructure between 2021/22 and 2024/25. By contrast, League Two clubs invested only £16m. Large clubs can also manage delays and rising costs, while smaller clubs have limited capacity to do so.

    Stadium investment key

    Luton Town is an example of this; the club announced plans to move from Kenilworth Road to Power Court in 2016 but since then the club has moved between divisions while the stadium project faced planning, legal and design hurdles. For smaller clubs such delays could be the difference between spades in the ground and nothing at all.

    The government must therefore step up and reduce some of the planning, transport, land and infrastructure barriers that hinder private investment. The Stadium Regeneration Accelerator announced earlier this year will offer a clear incentive to focus on the largest projects. But the true measure of the initiative is whether government involvement enables projects to go ahead that otherwise would not.

    Stadium investment is part of the solution to a problem that plagues most of the sport. The government should continue supporting major regeneration schemes that create housing, jobs and investment, but the opportunity extends further. The true value of the Stadium Regeneration Accelerator lies in helping viable projects lower down the pyramid overcome barriers that clubs cannot address alone. This would not only support regeneration around football grounds but also help vulnerable clubs build stronger businesses.

    Joseph Smith is a senior consultant at Henham Strategy

    Lawyers have been warned they remain accountable for supervising AI use within their law firm, particularly when junior employees are operating the technology.

    The Law Society, an independent body that represents solicitors in England and Wales, issued new guidance on Wednesday setting out the appropriate use of AI in legal work, meaning lawyers cannot blame the technology – or junior employees – for any mistakes it makes.

    The guidance states that lawyers’ “professional duties and obligations apply in the same way whether AI or other technologies were used” by the solicitor themselves “or by anyone under that solicitor’s supervision to assist with that work.”

    Vice-Chair of the City of London Law Society’s AI Committee Kerry Westland, told City AM that while AI “has significant potential to support lawyers at every level” it “does not displace firms’ existing duties of competence, supervision and accountability.”

    “Firms will need to ensure that junior lawyers are trained to use AI critically and safely, while continuing to develop the legal judgement and practical skills that come from properly supervised experience. The Committee will consider the guidance as part of its ongoing work on the impact of AI across CLLS member firms,” Westland said.

    The Law Society added that AI is “no substitute for junior lawyers” and those which are responsible for junior colleagues must make sure the tech does not “replace opportunities”, including how to “identify errors, omissions and unsupported propositions.”

    “Solicitors and law firms should choose their AI tools carefully and always check that legal work meets their professional standards. Over-reliance on AI systems may result in a catastrophic gap of future legal skills and knowledge,” Brett Dixon, president of the Law Society, said.

    The legal watchdog, the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), issued a similar warning in August noting that lawyers who supervise junior colleagues “may also be found to have breached regulatory requirements and professional duties if false citations are put before the court without adequate review and/or supervision.”

    Legal sectors’ AI use under the microscope

    This comes as lawyers and law firms across London and the rest of the UK are being closely watched by the courts and legal regulators and reprimanded for any mistakes made in AI-assisted legal work.

    In September, an immigration lawyer, Abhisek Kumar, who was referred to a Tribunal after a criminal conviction became the first solicitor in the UK to be struck off after using AI-generated evidence as part of his own defence.

    The Upper Tribunal issued a warning earlier this year in an immigration case on the serious risks of using AI in court documents, including in legal professional privilege.

    The lawyers had either used AI themselves or instructed their junior staff to use it to draft an immigration judicial review application which contained inaccurate citations of case law.

    Lewisham’s £1.5bn shopping centre redevelopment freeze, caused by a breakdown between Landsec and the Council, has left residents, traders, and the town centre stranded in uncertainty, says Sergiy Lesyk

    Lewisham shows how a council can lose a £1.5bn scheme and gain nothing.

    Landsec, the property company that has owned Lewisham Shopping Centre for more than 20 years, has put its £1.5bn redevelopment of the centre on hold. Councillors approved the scheme in October 2025, and work had been due to start in 2027. Now nobody can say when, or whether, anything will happen.

    You don’t have to have liked the plans to see the problem that residents and traders in Lewisham now face.

    Landsec gave two reasons: one was the cost of building in London, the other was the Council. In Landsec’s words, recent statements from the Council “make clear that the administration is not able to support the next phase of land assembly needed to unlock delivery without a significant increase in affordable housing.”

    On a social video, the mayor, Liam Shrivastava, had the temerity to state “the conditions for such developments are simply not favourable right now”, and that “the way out of the housing crisis is through building social housing.”

    The mayor was elected on a promise of 1,000 new social rent homes. Instead, the plan to replace the shopping centre with 1,744 homes, including 98 for social rent and 231 at discounted rents or for key workers, will no longer be built. The shopping centre development took about five years to approve, so who really thinks this council will match it any time soon?

    Boots has left its high street unit, which sits in the first phase, for a unit inside the centre. Marks & Spencer, a fixture in Lewisham for almost a century, has closed for good, Natwest has said it will close its branch, and the Model Market food hall still hasn’t reopened.

    Landsec itself says the 1970s building is no longer fit for purpose, as it had been expected to be demolished. 

    Labour, which approved the scheme, and the Greens, who now run the Council, are busy blaming each other, and the mayor is blaming the government. Finger-pointing won’t build a single home or fill a single empty unit.

    Lewisham is being let down

    And the drift goes well beyond the shopping centre. A short walk away, the 649 homes of the Filigree at Lewisham Gateway have stood empty since a flood in February 2025, and residents won’t be back before October 2027. Nearby, one resident told us that food waste bins turned up at their block with no guidance and no collections. The building manager has had to tell everyone not to use them until the council explains what happens next. Even the council’s own website can’t seem to agree on whether flats are getting food waste collections.

    This matters well beyond SE13. London needs homes, and it needs investors with the long-term support and confidence of local councils to build them. 

    So what should happen now?

    First, the council should be straight with residents about what it told Landsec and what it now expects to happen to the site.

    Second, it should publish a support plan for the traders caught up in the uncertainty, because they’re paying for decisions they didn’t make.

    Third, and most importantly, it should set out its own plan for Lewisham town centre. If this scheme wasn’t good enough, the Council needs to show what would be, who will build it, and when.

    Lewisham Conservatives support homes and investment in Lewisham, but not a town centre left in limbo. Residents were promised new homes, a new town centre and a new community. They’ve been let down. The council can’t build any of it until it first rebuilds their trust.

    Sergiy Lesyk is chairman of Lewisham Conservatives

    Rathbones posted a rise in funds under management and administration as its wealth management arm returned to net inflows.

    Funds under management and adminsitration increased 7.2 per cent year on year to £121.1bn.

    Its wealth management arm achieved net inflows, increasing to £24m after reporting losses of £300m the previous year. 

    Further growth was restricted after the FTSE 250 firm’s voluntary pause on accepting new money from enhanced due diligence (EDD) clients.

    The firm also pinned the further lack of inflows on “a cautious backdrop” in the run up to the looming Autumn Budget which has caused clients to delay allocating capital to their portfolios.

    But despite the rise in wealth management, clients withdrew a total net £401m from the company during the period, after increased pressure on its asset management channel.

    Its asset management arm reported outflows of £425m, reflecting “continued pressure” on active equity investment in the UK retail market. Gross outflows reached £738m.

    Rathbones shares nudged up 1.2 per cent to 1,618p. The stock is down by 15 per cent since the start of the year.

    FCA update

    Rathbone’s subsidiary, Vision Independent Financial Planning, received a Section 166 notice from the City watchdog in August, which requires the FTSE 250 firm to conduct a “Skilled Person” review into the business.

    The order forces businesses to appoint independent advisers to carry out a probe into the operations of the company and is used to determine whether the regulator will take enforcement action.

    The provision is estimated to cost Rathbones £2.5m. The business’ future pre-tax profit is also expected to reduce by £4m from 2027 onwards due to the decline in the number of adviser firms working with them.

    Rathbones will continue to manage its £1.9bn funds under management and administration (FUMA) for clients tied to the firm.

    ‘Good progress’

    Rathbones itself was subject to a review from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) which is expected to rack up costs of up to £60m, after the watchdog uncovered compliance shortcoming earlier this year.

    In response, the group stopped onboarding new enhanced due diligence (EDD) clients, but it expects to lift restrictions on EDD in the fourth quarter, and said it has made “good progress” to address the findings in the Skilled Person review.

    Rathbones confirmed the regulatory programme in June continues on schedule, while targeted client reviews have also started. It said no “material client outflows were attributable to the programme”.

    Chief executive, Jonathan Sorrell, also doubled down on his commitment to turn Rathbones into “the best wealth manager in the UK” despite the FCA reviews.
