Choose the commutation method according to motion quality

Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior.

Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations.

Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning.

Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components.

The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM).

In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM.

FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications.

FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error.

Select the feedback architecture

Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems.

Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information.

Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence.

Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important.

The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position.

That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase.

Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy.

Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate.

Match the controller to the robotic arm

A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback.

A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control.

This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task.

An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller.

The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier.

The Robot Report‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components.

For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function.

Match the controller to the mobile robot

BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment.

A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide.

Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods of sustained power.

Battery behavior also changes the controller decision. Voltage sag under acceleration reduces the available electrical headroom, while regenerative braking can raise DC bus voltage. A controller designed around a nominal battery voltage therefore needs to be evaluated over the complete battery operating range rather than at one nominal value.

Thermal design is another difference. A drive enclosed inside a wheel or compact chassis may have limited airflow. The inverter, motor windings, bearings, connectors, and mechanical structure all become part of the heat path.

Harmonic Drive‘s servo-grade propulsion drive trains for AMRs illustrate this system-level relationship. Their characteristics include smooth travel, backdrivability, torque density, stiffness, and radial load support. The lesson is not that one transmission is appropriate for every AMR, but that propulsion control cannot be separated from the drivetrain.

Mobile manipulators make the distinction even more obvious. Desmasa’s MCR+ combined a robot arm and an AMR that shared one power and control architecture. The drive requirements of the base remained different from those of the arm, even though both ultimately contained electric actuators.

Evaluate current sensing and thermal behavior

Controller current ratings require careful interpretation. A datasheet may list continuous phase current, continuous bus current, peak phase current, peak current duration, RMS current, or a configurable current limit. These numbers are not interchangeable.

The motor’s thermal limit, inverter semiconductor limit, connector rating, cable rating, and battery capability can all be lower than a headline peak current specification. A controller advertised with a large peak current is therefore not automatically suitable for a motor that requires that current continuously.

BLDC.com provides a useful commercial example of the specification categories engineers encounter in controller selection. Its current controller catalog lists different input voltage ranges and current ratings across several controller families, while individual products describe interfaces and protection features.

Those specifications illustrate why engineers should compare voltage range, current definition, duration, feedback compatibility, and protection functions rather than simply comparing wattage.

The heat path must also be considered. Motor winding losses have to leave the motor through its structure and mounting arrangement. Power stage losses must leave the inverter through its enclosure, thermal interface, heat sink, airflow, or mounting structure. Thermal testing under the actual duty cycle is more informative than relying only on a short unloaded bench test.

Consider the communications and software layers

The motor controller is normally responsible for the fastest control loops. A robot controller does not need to calculate every PWM transition. Instead, the drive can execute current regulation and commutation locally while receiving higher level torque, velocity, or position commands.

Before selecting a drive, engineers should check CAN or CANopen support, EtherCAT support, RS 485 or UART, analog and PWM inputs, encoder interfaces, feedback update rates, command latency, fault reporting, firmware update procedures, parameter storage, multi axis synchronization, ROS 2 or ros2_control integration, and CiA 402 support where applicable.

CANopen’s CiA 402 profile standardizes functional behavior for servo drives and other motion control devices, including operating states and command/status structures. That can simplify interoperability when the selected hardware actually implements the required profile.

EtherCAT becomes attractive when synchronized multi axis motion and deterministic timing are central requirements. Its distributed clock architecture allows participating devices to synchronize their local timing.

ROS 2 integration is a separate consideration from the physical bus. Ros2_control represents robot hardware through command and state interfaces and provides a framework for connecting controllers to physical actuators. The controller manager also emphasizes deterministic control loop execution, showing why communication availability alone does not guarantee real time behavior.

Treat safety as an architecture, not a checkbox

A motor controller should be evaluated for overcurrent, short circuit, overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, overspeed, encoder failure, Hall failure, phase loss, stall detection, brake control, communications loss, regenerative voltage rise, unintended restart, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque off where applicable.

These functions are not automatically equivalent to a complete safety architecture. Safety requirements depend on the robot category, risk assessment, operating environment, and system design.

For industrial robots, ISO 10218 1:2025 specifies safety requirements for industrial robots. ISO 13849 1:2023 addresses the design of safety related parts of control systems, including software. IEC 61800 5 2 addresses functional safety considerations for safety related adjustable speed power drive systems.

The important engineering distinction is that a controller having an overcurrent shutdown or temperature sensor does not, by itself, establish a certified safety function. The safety function has to be designed, validated, and integrated according to the applicable requirements.

A practical selection workflow

A useful motor controller selection process can be reduced to ten engineering steps.

  • Step 1: Define the complete load and motion profile, including acceleration, deceleration, payload, terrain, gravity, and duty cycle.
  • Step 2: Calculate continuous and peak torque at the motor shaft and, where applicable, at the joint or wheel.
  • Step 3: Establish the required speed, acceleration, operating range, and regenerative braking conditions.
  • Step 4: Define the control objective: speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction.
  • Step 5: Select feedback according to the actual control objective and mechanical transmission.
  • Step 6: Select six step, sinusoidal, or FOC control based on motion quality, speed range, torque requirements, and implementation constraints.
  • Step 7: Check voltage, continuous and peak current, regeneration, thermal margins, and battery behavior.
  • Step 8: Select the communication and software interfaces needed by the robot architecture.
  • Step 9: Define safety behavior, fault response, braking, communication loss behavior, and restart conditions.
  • Step 10: Validate the complete motor, drive, gearbox, sensor, brake, and robot controller as one system.

BLDC motor control selection decision table

Application requirement Preferred control direction Main reason Important limitation
Simple wheel speed control Sensored six step or simple closed loop control Low implementation complexity Coarser torque and position behavior
High-efficiency mobile traction FOC with appropriate feedback Good torque and speed regulation across a wide operating range Higher software and tuning complexity
Low-speed robotic joint motion Encoder based FOC Smooth torque production and precise rotor angle information Transmission and tuning still limit performance
High precision joint positioning Servo drive with encoder feedback, potentially output feedback Position loop can account for joint behavior More sensors, wiring, and integration effort
Torque controlled collaborative joint FOC servo architecture with suitable torque feedback or estimation Fast current/torque response Safety and torque accuracy require system validation
Sensorless high speed drive Sensorless commutation or sensorless FOC Eliminates position sensors and wiring Startup and very low speed behavior require careful design
Multi axis synchronized arm Networked servo drives, often with deterministic Ethernet Coordinated timing and distributed control Network and drive configuration become part of commissioning
Harsh outdoor mobile robot Closed loop drive with feedback selected for the environment Better speed control, diagnostics, and traction management Environmental sealing and thermal design remain system level issues

Commissioning and validation

A controller should not move directly from a wiring diagram to production operation. First, verify phase order and encoder direction. Confirm Hall or encoder alignment and current sense polarity. Run the motor unloaded at reduced voltage where the hardware permits it, then compare commanded and measured speed.

Next, check position error and current behavior. Apply a controlled mechanical load and measure phase current and bus current. Monitor motor and inverter temperatures during acceleration, steady operation, and repeated cycles.

Regenerative braking deserves a dedicated test. Measure the DC bus during controlled deceleration and confirm that the battery, braking circuit, and controller remain within their operating limits.

Communication loss testing should verify what the drive actually does when commands stop arriving. Sensor disconnection tests should confirm fault detection and the resulting state. Overcurrent, thermal protection, emergency stop, and brake behavior should also be tested under controlled conditions.

Finally, repeat the important tests after thermal soak. A drive that behaves correctly for several minutes at room temperature may behave differently after the motor and inverter reach their operating temperatures.

For a robotic arm, these tests should be performed with the gearbox and representative mechanism installed. For a mobile robot, they should include the actual wheel, vehicle mass, battery, terrain, and representative duty cycle. A bench test of an unloaded motor validates only part of the system.

Engineer’s checklist

  1. What are the continuous and peak torque requirements?
  2. What is the required speed and acceleration range?
  3. Is the objective speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction control?
  4. Is Hall feedback sufficient, or is encoder feedback required?
  5. Is motor side feedback sufficient for the mechanical transmission?
  6. Does six step control provide adequate motion quality, or is FOC justified?
  7. Are voltage, current, regeneration, and thermal margins adequate?
  8. Does the communications interface meet latency and synchronization requirements?
  9. What happens during sensor failure, communication loss, braking, and emergency stop?
  10. Has the complete actuator been tested under the actual mechanical duty cycle?

Pulling together criteria to pick the right motor

The correct BLDC motor control architecture is determined by the control variable, mechanical transmission, feedback quality, duty cycle, thermal limits, energy system, safety architecture, and software integration.

For a simple mobile drive, a sensored six-step controller may provide an adequate combination of cost, robustness, and speed regulation. A demanding robotic joint may instead require encoder based FOC, nested torque, velocity, and position loops, and possibly output side feedback.

An outdoor mobile platform may need closed loop traction control, careful regenerative energy management, environmental protection, and thermal capacity that would be unnecessary on a small indoor robot.

The key decision is therefore not simply which BLDC motor controller has the right voltage or wattage rating. The useful question is whether the complete motor, inverter, feedback system, transmission, power source, communications layer, and safety architecture can produce the required behavior throughout the robot’s actual operating envelope.

The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI.

AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world.

Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report. Success will depend on more than model performance. It will require advances across sensing, simulation, computing, connectivity, and control.

In many cases, the technologies that determine whether a system succeeds sit beneath the application layer itself. A machine that shuts down when vibration crosses a preset limit is following a rule. A machine that reads vibration, temperature, current, and motor behavior; recognizes the signature of bearing wear; and adjusts before failure occurs is doing something closer to judgment.

That distinction helps explain why physical AI has become one of the most closely watched areas in technology for manufacturing. These systems do more than analyze information. They interact with the world around them, adapting to changing conditions and responding to situations that cannot be fully predicted in advance.

The next phase of physical and embodied AI is not simply about producing better answers. It is about predicting and producing useful actions in the presence of imperfect information, said ADI. To read the full whitepaper, click here: The Race to Make AI Physical.

]]> Europe’s technology ecosystem is evolving rapidly, with AI, FinTech, DeepTech and digital regulation dominating headlines and reshaping the industry. Behind these stories is a network of journalists and communications professionals who play a vital role in how Europe’s technology sector is reported on, understood and represented.

From reporters breaking stories on Europe’s biggest Tech companies and emerging startups to PR leaders building the profiles of ambitious businesses, these individuals help shape the conversation around European innovation.

This list brings together influential voices from leading publications and communications agencies specialising in Tech. Spanning the UK, Ireland and continental Europe, the list highlights professionals covering and communicating some of the industry’s most important developments.

Presented in alphabetical order, rather than as a ranking, the list celebrates the people helping to tell Europe’s technology stories.

Adam Satariano is a Technology Correspondent at The New York Times, covering European digital policy and the intersection of technology and world affairs, with a focus on regulation, AI, privacy and Tech geopolitics.

 

Adrian Weckler is Technology Editor at the Irish Independent and host of The Big Tech Show, covering everything from AI and big Tech to startups, telecoms and consumer technology.

 

Akansha Dimri is the founder and Editor-in-Chief of Tech Funding News, covering European technology startups, venture capital and funding developments, with a focus on FinTech, AI, DeepTech, HealthTech and the wider startup ecosystem.

 

Alex Warren is Head of Content & Creative at Wildfire, leading content strategy and creative campaigns for B2B technology brands, with expertise in AI, MarTech and technology communications.

 

Alexander Hüsing is an Editor at Deutsche Startups, covering Germany’s startup ecosystem and the wider European technology landscape, with a focus on venture capital, funding rounds, entrepreneurship and the digital economy.

 

Amy Lewin is Editor at Sifted, leading its coverage of Europe’s startup and venture capital ecosystem. She also hosts Startup Europe — The Sifted Podcast and covers AI, FinTech, investment trends and European technology policy.

 

Ana Marija Kostanic is Editor-in-Chief at The Recursive, covering Southeast Europe’s growing startup and technology ecosystem, with a focus on AI, venture capital and innovation.

 

Ana-Maria Stanciuc is Editor-in-Chief at The Next Web, overseeing coverage of Europe’s technology industry, including startups, venture capital and entrepreneurship.

]]> The CLARITY Act was designed to set clearer rules for how digital assets are classified and overseen in the US. Its failure in the Senate leaves American investors without that framework for now, and anyone watching the Ethereum price USD chart saw the reaction within hours.

The much-lauded CLARITY Act failed to advance in the US Senate on Tuesday, September 15, in a severe setback for the digital assets and crypto industry. It fell 11 votes short of the 60-vote threshold it needed to move onward in the 100-seat chamber. Primarily put forward by Republican lawmakers, three of them voted against it, joining every Senate Democrat in opposition, and the motion failed. The impact will be felt by anyone who trades digital assets, in the US and abroad.

How did markets respond to the Clarity Act failure?

Markets responded quickly to the news. Binance market data showed Bitcoin dropping 5% after the vote. At the time of writing (September 18), it had rebounded slightly, climbing to $78,180 from a $75,390 low on Tuesday, September 15. Ether stood at $2,515, up from $2,378 the day after the vote. Share prices of several crypto firms also fell, with Coinbase and Circle each down about 10%, according to Cointelegraph.

This will push any further decisions on it until after the mid-term elections, which will take place in November. A key fight to take control of the House and Senate, it could potentially be pushed back until 2029 should Democrats make it a priority and stop it dead in its tracks.

What was the Clarity Act?

The CLARITY Act was an attempt to provide a US federal framework for digital asset markets. For years, there has been confusion over where digital assets lie in the US and who has oversight for them. Primarily, this was the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Where value is derived from network use and trading, in spot markets, jurisdiction would have been given to the CFTC. The SEC would have had an overview of digital securities in which the value depended on a specific company’s managerial efforts.

How have banks reacted to the Clarity Act news?

The US Banking lobby has already pledged its support to keep fighting for the bill. This is mainly because it still leaves questions around stablecoin yields unanswered. A joint statement from the Independent Community Bankers of America and American Bankers Association noted that “as lawmakers consider next steps, we encourage them to adopt targeted changes to stablecoin yield policy.”

It is likely this will now pivot the conversation to how banks can begin to implement the GENIUS Act. Signed into law in 2025, it has barred stablecoin issuers from offering rewards. Yet it does allow third parties, such as exchanges, to pay yields. The Independent Community Bankers of America has warned that this could drain as much as $1.3 trillion from community bank deposits.

Stablecoin builders outside the US are watching this fight closely: EU-Startups reported in July 2025 that London fintech Due had raised €6.3 million and launched a stablecoin API for borderless payments, the kind of product whose US reach depends on how Washington settles yield.

How did crypto exchanges react?

The major crypto exchanges were keen to point out that by no means does this signal the end for the CLARITY Act. Binance added that “With the November midterm elections approaching, lawmakers have limited time to resolve disagreements and secure the votes needed to move the bill forward. A renewed attempt would still have to navigate Senate procedures and any remaining legislative steps, including resolving differences with the House-passed version before legislation could reach the president.” They then closed this with “The immediate result is a stalled bill, not necessarily a permanently dead one.”

Other crypto companies also released statements on the event. Ripple described this as a “tremendous missed opportunity” in a statement on their website. They went on to add that “Consumers and market participants still deserve predictable standards and protections. Responsible businesses should not have to rely on years of litigation or live under the threat of one to understand how the law applies to them. And the United States should not concede leadership in the future of finance because policymakers were unable to establish a durable framework. Ripple will continue advocating for market structure legislation and engaging constructively with policymakers.”

This will only add to the volatility the crypto market has displayed over the last few months. Rising oil prices and expectations that the Federal Reserve would hike rates, which it did on Wednesday, September 16, have also weighed on sentiment.

Further dampening the mood were comments signaling that investors should not write off the prospect of another rate raise before the year is out. This was the first rate rise in three years, taking them to 3.75%-4%, according to the Federal Reserve’s September 16 statement, as reported by CNBC. After the September 16 decision, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long“, then branded the move a “sober” and “responsible decision“. He then highlighted that inflation remains a problem, showing that more may yet be due to come.

]]> NEURA Robotics continues its roll of recent announcements with the launch of a new robot and the opening of a new branch of their Neura Gym in partnership with the Technical University of Munich (TUM).

The two have today opened the TUM RoboGym powered by NEURA at LabCampus near Munich Airport. Spanning more than 2,300 square meters, the new centre brings together research, robot training and industrial application.

It was built in partnership with TUM’s Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI). The joint initiative is initially set up for three years. In total, the partners are investing around €17 million, of which NEURA is contributing approximately €11 million.

To mark the opening, NEURA is also launching 4NE1 Gen 4 (“For Anyone”), the new generation of its humanoid robot.

“Our companies hold knowledge that has been built up over generations,” says David Reger, founder and CEO of NEURA Robotics. “People know how to work materials, assemble components and master difficult processes. This knowledge is one of our greatest strengths in the age of Physical AI. With TUM, we are building a powerhouse for physical capabilities, where this knowledge becomes the foundation for new possibilities. The Mittelstand, in particular, should be able to help shape this future.

“With the launch of the humanoid 4NE1 Gen 4, we are showing today which robots are ready for it: designed for series production, built for productive work and powered by Neuron AI, our own foundation model that learns from experience in the NEURA Gyms. Developed, built and trained in Germany, for the world.”

Across Europe, other robotics companies are pursuing similar efforts to bring adaptable machines into industrial environments.

London-based Humanoid raised €133 million in July to advance its humanoid robots, while fellow German companies Sereact and RobCo, itself a TUM spin-out, secured €93 million and €89.2 million respectively to develop physical AI and autonomous industrial systems.

Spain’s THEKER added €73 million for AI-native industrial robots, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics raised €26 million to develop adaptable robot skills.

Alongside smaller rounds for Poland’s Nomagic, Hungary’s Allonic and Belgium’s Motion, these 2026 rounds total approximately €430.2 million.

“The TUM RoboGym robotics center is unique in Germany and Europe,” adds Prof. Thomas Hofmann, President of the Technical University of Munich. “By collaborating with a robot manufacturer based in Germany, we are also sending a clear signal for Germany as an industrial location in geopolitically uncertain times.”

Today’s partnerships marks an even closer relationship between one of Germany’s premier Unicorns with what is arguably the country’s foremost tech/innovation university.

Founded in 2019, Neura develops the technologies that enable intelligent machines to learn, adapt and work side by side with humans in the real world. The company develops cognitive robots that can see, hear, feel and learn, as well as the software, AI and data infrastructure required for their large-scale deployment.

On the education side, TUM MIRMI is an integrative research institute of the TUM focused on robotics and AI. MIRMI holds leading expertise in key areas of robotics, including perception and data science. Nearly 80 TUM chairs are networked within TUM MIRMI to develop robotic and AI-supported solutions for the environment, health, mobility, labor, and security and defense.

The TUM RoboGym brings together AI research and industrial application. Companies contribute concrete tasks and their process knowledge. Researchers and development teams investigate how robots can learn these tasks faster and perform them more reliably.

Partners have been training concrete workflows at the TUM RoboGym since September. Companies from more than ten industries are involved, including automotive, pharmaceuticals, medical technology, packaging, logistics, agriculture and care. Demand is high: capacity in Munich is already in strong demand.

Tasks range from handling cardboard boxes and filling bottles to loading and unloading wooden components. Companies can test applications, identify training needs and assess the suitability of different robot systems before expanding use in their own operations.

The RoboGym combines three approaches to generating data:

  • Real-world robot data: Different robot systems perform tasks. Their sensors capture movements, contacts and the outcomes of their actions.
  • Human demonstrations: People demonstrate workflows. Sensor-equipped data suits, motion-capture systems and teleoperation help translate movements and interactions into usable training data.
  • Simulation and Data Amplifier: Virtual training environments expand real-world experience with additional variations and situations, allowing skills to be trained under changed conditions and then validated on real robots.

With 4NE1 Gen 4, NEURA is launching the new generation of its humanoid robot, already in operation at the TUM RoboGym for the opening: slimmer, lighter and powered by Neuron AI as its brain.

Alongside the opening of the TUM RoboGym in Munich, the robot is also appearing at the NVIDIA GTC conference in Berlin and is already in operation at the NEURA Gyms.

“We want companies to carry their experience into the next industrial era,” says David. “To develop capabilities, protect their know-how and decide for themselves, in the future, where and under what conditions they make it available to others. What we are opening today in Munich is meant to have an impact far beyond this location. From Europe, together for the world.”

The TUM RoboGym marks the start of an international network of NEURA Gyms. Further locations are being established in Europe, the United States and China. In Germany, another Gym is being built in cooperation with RWTH Aachen.

]]> Indurex, an Amsterdam-based startup building an AI-native platform for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) security, has raised €7 million in funding, less than nine months after coming out of stealth.

The round was led by Contrarian Ventures, the European early-stage firm that backs energy and industrial technology companies, with participation from Axeleo Capital and Dutch venture capital firm Curiosity. 

“Electrification is putting more critical infrastructure online, and attacks on it are rising, with the damage felt in the physical world: cold homes, dark hospitals, water that stops flowing. Detection alone is no longer enough. Operators need to understand what an alert means for the physical process behind it. Having built and sold a company in this space, Jalal knows what operators across oil and gas, power and manufacturing need, which makes Indurex one of very few companies that understands both the network packet and the physical process,” said Rokas Peciulaitis, Founder and Managing Partner at Contrarian Ventures.

Indurex was founded by Jalal Bouhdada and Maarten Oosterink, seasoned practitioners in operational technology (OT), process safety, and cybersecurity. The company launched in January 2026 with a stated goal of keeping complex cyber-physical systems resilient, safe, and secure for operators in oil and gas, energy, utilities, manufacturing, and data centres. The company brings together cybersecurity, process safety, and engineering operations under a single layer of intelligence called Engineering Intelligence.

Its offering is called Indurex SafeGuard AI, a platform that ingests data from distributed control systems, safety instrumented systems, historians, alarm management systems, and IT security tools. It then uses AI agents to surface anomalies and engineering deviations, giving operators a unified view that links cybersecurity alerts directly to the physical process behind them, something conventional OT security systems have failed to address.

“Cyber defences in these critical sectors have focused solely on the network. We focus on the core industrial data itself: the engineering, process and safety signals that determine whether a plant is operating within safe limits. Cybersecurity and operational excellence have too often been managed as separate disciplines — Engineering Intelligence is the missing layer, and this funding allows us to bring that capability to more operators across critical infrastructure,” said Bouhdada, co-founder and CEO of Indurex.

Indurex says its early customers range from mid-sized energy and manufacturing companies to large multinational enterprises. With Indurex’s AI platform, these customers are reportedly seeing value across three areas: operational excellence and safety integrity, through unified situational awareness; cyber resilience via detection and response aligned to operational and safety impact; and compliance through automated reporting against frameworks including IEC 62443, IEC 61511/61508, NIS2, NIST CSF and NERC CIP.

The funding comes as cyber threats to industrial environments intensify. According to the SANS Institute’s State of ICS/OT Security 2025 survey, more than one in five industrial organisations experienced an ICS or OT cyber incident in the past year, with 40% of those incidents disrupting operations and close to 20% taking more than a month to fully remediate.

Indurex says it will deploy the fresh capital toward research and development and expand its commercial operations across Europe and the Middle East, ahead of a subsequent expansion into the United States and Asia-Pacific.

]]> It should come as no surprise to hear that the UK is growing from strength to strength when it comes to startup investment, with new research revealing billions in funding for university spinouts, larger investment rounds in Cambridge and a wave of funding for DefenceTech.

But while investors appear increasingly willing to back established, capital-intensive businesses, the figures also reveal a growing challenge for startups seeking their first investment.

Three recently published studies from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), Parkwalk and Beauhurst, and White & Case offer a common thread connecting the British funding landscape in 2026.

The numbers are notable. UK university spinouts secured €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) in the first half of 2026, Greater Cambridge’s early-stage businesses have raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015, and 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and technology startups expect to seek significant external funding over the next 12 months.

So, is Britain Europe’s leading startup investment destination?

Universities and their billion-pound momentum

Greater Cambridge is one of the clearest examples of the UK’s growing capacity to attract investment into technology companies.

According to analysis published by Cambridge Innovation Capital for the Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026, early-stage businesses in the region have collectively raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015.

More significantly, the average equity raised per deal has increased fivefold over the decade, rising from €2.3 million (£2 million) in 2015 to €11 million (£10 million) in 2025. Greater Cambridge’s life sciences and DeepTech businesses also reportedly attracted more funding per deal on average in 2025 than their counterparts in London, Greater Oxford and Greater Manchester.

The findings suggest that Cambridge is developing beyond its traditional role as a university research hub into an ecosystem capable of producing companies that attract larger investment rounds.

Cambridge’s momentum is reflected in several startups previously covered by EU-Startups. Battery technology company Nyobolt raised €26.3 million in April 2025, before reaching a $1 billion valuation in 2026. Meanwhile, AI materials discovery startup CuspAI secured €393.2 million in July 2026 at a €2.2 billion valuation, while launching an AI Materials Foundry involving NVIDIA.

More recently, DefenceTech company Cambridge Aerospace raised €259.7 million in August 2026 at a €2.94 billion valuation.

Dr Michael Anstey, Partner at Cambridge Innovation Capital and board member Innovate Cambridge, said: “A fivefold increase in average deal size over ten years shows how far Cambridge’s innovation economy has matured. Investors are backing Cambridge companies with larger rounds because there is now a proven route from world-class research to businesses that can scale globally.” 

The growing size of Cambridge investment rounds reflects a wider pattern across UK university spinouts.

Research from Parkwalk and private company data provider Beauhurst found that UK university spinouts raised €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) across 215 deals in H1 2026, the second-highest half-year total recorded over the past decade and a 38.2% increase on H2 2025.

Much of this funding went into advanced technologies. Four companies alone – Quantum Motion, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Fractile and CellCentric – accounted for €846 million (£709 million), with Oxford Quantum Circuits securing the period’s largest round at €301 million (£260 million).

Defence funding takes off

Beyond university spinouts, another sector attracting investor attention is defence technology.

New research from White & Case reveals that 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and DefenceTech startups are likely to raise significant external funding over the next 12 months.

The study, conducted by Censuswide among 250 senior decision-makers in the UK defence and military sector between 17 and 24 September 2026, suggests that companies are preparing to scale in response to growing demand for advanced defence capabilities.

Businesses are considering a range of financing options, including equity investment, debt and government grants. Among surveyed companies, 49% intend to seek equity financing, 47% debt financing and 39% government grants.

Equity is particularly relevant to DefencetTech startups, with 59% considering this funding route, compared with 49% of established defence companies. Many younger businesses are still developing their products and have yet to generate significant revenues, making traditional debt financing more difficult.

Government-backed investors were identified as the most attractive equity funding source by 37% of businesses seeking equity, followed closely by corporate venture investors, strategic corporate investors and private equity firms.

Daniel Turgel, Partner and Co-head of White & Case’s Global Technology Industry Group, commented: “For the most promising businesses, there is no lack of equity financing. A wall of private capital is looking for a home in defence technology as previous investment restrictions are relaxed and investors rush to gain exposure to a highly attractive sector, with long-term structural growth tailwinds that extend beyond current conflicts and even defence itself.”

The findings suggest that DefenceTech could become another important contributor to UK startup investment, alongside established areas such as FinTech and life sciences.

Interest is being supported by rising military expenditure, government efforts to develop domestic technological capabilities and the potential dual-use applications of technologies initially developed for defence.

Big cheques, fewer first rounds

While the total value of investment into UK university spinouts is approaching record levels, the Parkwalk and Beauhurst findings reveal a more complicated picture for early-stage founders.

First-time equity investment fell from €176 million (£148 million) in H1 2025 to €56 million (£47 million) in H1 2026, a decline of 68.3%.

The number of first-time funding deals also decreased, from 47 to 44 over the same period, significantly below the peak of 73 recorded in H1 2021.

Meanwhile, later-stage investment reached €907 million (£760 million) in H1 2026, its highest half-year level since 2021, representing a 165% year-on-year increase.

The contrast is significant. Although more capital is flowing into established university spinouts, fewer emerging businesses are securing their first equity investment.

Moray Wright, CEO of Parkwalk, said: “British DeepTech is attracting capital at a scale we have rarely seen, and that is something to celebrate. But these figures carry a clear warning. First-time investment has fallen, and the companies vital to the future of the UK economy are struggling to raise their first round.”

The shift is also visible in average deal sizes, which have more than doubled over the past decade, from €4.2 million (£3.57 million) in H1 2016 to €8.6 million (£7.24 million) in H1 2026.

The growth of later-stage financing is a positive sign for the UK, but the shrinking pool of first-time funding raises questions about whether the country is building a sufficiently broad pipeline of new businesses to sustain its investment momentum.

Global money, British innovation

Another finding connecting the three studies is the UK’s growing relationship with international investors.

According to Parkwalk and Beauhurst, funding rounds involving at least one international investor accounted for 86.1% of total university spinout investment in H1 2026, the highest share recorded this decade.

British investors nevertheless remain central to the ecosystem. Since 2016, UK investors have participated in 2,545 spinout deals, more than six times the 408 involving US investors.

Yet international investment also introduces questions about where the value generated by British innovation ultimately ends up.

International buyers accounted for 75% of UK spinout acquisitions in H1 2026 and 68.3% of acquisitions since 2016. Over the decade, US buyers acquired 66 UK spinouts, compared with 57 acquired by British buyers.

The geographical distribution of funding presents another challenge. Nearly 80% of spinout investment since 2016 has gone to the South East, East of England and London.

University of Oxford spinouts have raised €6.4 billion (£5.39 billion) over this period, compared with €4.7 billion (£3.99 billion) for University of Cambridge spinouts. Further north, Manchester university spinouts attracted €232 million (£195 million), while those in Liverpool secured €23.3 million (£19.6 million).

So, on top of there being a clear difficulty in directing funding to early-stage companies, there seems to be a higher amount of foreign investment circulating than national funding across an imbalanced geography. Bringing into question the future interests of these companies, their investors and eventual market goals.

Conclusion

Wether the UK can translate their clear financial strength into long-term European leadership will depend on more than headline investment totals.

Ensuring early-stage founders can access funding, encouraging investment beyond established innovation hubs and helping British companies remain and grow in the country will be equally important.

The UK’s startup funding lead does not simply depend on how much capital it can attract, but how widely that capital can support the next generation of companies.

]]> Enact Intelligence, a physical AI startup headquartered in Zurich, has come out of stealth today with a €26.68 million ($30 million) pre-Seed funding round, one of the largest pre-Seed raises in Europe to date.

The round saw participation from institutional investors redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital, alongside a notable slate of angel investors, including Arthur Mensch, founder of Mistral; Yann LeCun, founder of AMI Labs and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta; and Andrew Lonsberry, founder of Path Robotics.

“Dexterity is the next frontier in robotics, and Enact is tackling it with a new data modality: starting with high precision force data from bespoke actuators they are rethinking the entire stack from the hardware up. We are very excited about Enact’s approach of leveraging orthogonal data to improve existing models and build a data moat,” said Dr. Harald Nieder, General Partner of redalpine.

Founded in March 2026 by Manuel Yves Galliker, Enact is building robots that can not only see their environment but physically sense what is happening when they interact with it. Before founding Enact, Galliker led the software team for the humanoid robot NEO at 1X, helped build 1X’s AI team in Silicon Valley, and went on to work at the robotics lab Physical Intelligence.

The central argument of Enact is that most robots today depend almost entirely on vision to perceive their surroundings, limiting their ability to manipulate objects reliably or learn efficiently from experience. Existing haptic sensing solutions, which extend robots with force and touch, are either too costly or fragile for meaningful industrial deployment.

To solve this physical AI challenge, Enact rethinks the entire stack, from model architectures and data pipelines through to the actuators and sensors that feed the model. As a departure from traditional robots relying on point-based force sensors, Enact’s robots capture force data directly from the actuators themselves, similar to how humans sense tension through their muscles rather than solely through their fingertips.

Manuel Yves Galliker, CEO and founder of Enact Intelligence, said, “Unlike the early days of LLMs, physical AI has the advantage of starting from strong reasoning, language, and vision capabilities already in place. Instead of trying to collect every piece of data needed to teach a robot common sense about the world, we can build on top of existing models, like video models, and adapt them to output robot actions for interacting with the real world. So what we are addressing is the ability to efficiently learn from experience and perform tasks reliably, both of which require the model to understand the physics of the robot and the task at hand.”

This approach, Galliker argues, will lead to the development of “a proprioceptive nerve system and the cortex that makes sense of it,” solving dexterity through whole-body force-awareness at a cost and reality-level suitable for industrial scale.

Enact’s twelve-person team draws its engineering talent from DeepMind, 1X, Amazon Robotics, Helsing, Physical Intelligence and ETH Zurich. Alongside the funding, the company announced bringing Philip Kneis, a former DeepTech investor at redalpine, to lead growth.

“Silicon Valley has traditionally been very strong in software and AI, but it’s lacking in robotics and hardware engineering talent, and with the current excitement around robotics a lot of money is chasing a few people. What we will do is bring the AI experience with us from Silicon Valley and combine it with Zürich’s local talent pool. That’s the winning formula,” added Galliker.

The fresh capital will be used to grow its team fivefold by the end of 2027, accelerate its hardware and R&D pipelines, and roll out its robots with multiple industrial partners across manufacturing, infrastructure, retail, and food processing.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:29:10 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 FAA orders inspections of nearly 2,000 Boeing 737 jets over potential loss-of-control risk https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/faa-inspections-boeing-737-control-issues/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:29:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54216 Nearly 2,000 US-registered Boeing 737NG aircraft will be inspected after the FAA identified a potential issue with a component used to control the aircraft's movement in flight.

The post FAA orders inspections of nearly 2,000 Boeing 737 jets over potential loss-of-control risk appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered mandatory inspections of nearly 2,000 Boeing 737 Next Generation (NG) aircraft after reports of pitch oscillations raised concerns about excessive movement in components controlling the aircraft’s horizontal stabiliser.

The new airworthiness directive, published in the Federal Register on 19 October, applies to certain Boeing 737-600, 737-700, 737-700C, 737-800, 737-900 and 737-900ER aircraft. The FAA estimates that 1,987 US-registered aircraft are affected.

The directive, designated AD 2026-20-14, will take effect on 23 November 2026 and requires operators to measure movement in the horizontal stabiliser pivot hinges and jackscrew, followed by inspections, repairs or replacement of components where necessary.

According to the FAA, excessive freeplay left unaddressed could lead to an aerodynamic flutter event, potentially resulting in loss of control of the aircraft.

What has prompted the FAA’s action?

The directive follows reports from multiple operators of pitch oscillation events associated with excessive horizontal stabiliser freeplay.

The horizontal stabiliser is mounted at the rear of the aircraft and helps control its pitch, or nose-up and nose-down movement. Its position is adjusted through a mechanical system that includes pivot hinges and a jackscrew.

Freeplay refers to unwanted movement or looseness within a mechanical connection. Although some movement is expected in mechanical systems, excessive freeplay can affect how components respond to aerodynamic forces.

If the movement exceeds prescribed limits, the aircraft may become more susceptible to flutter – a potentially dangerous phenomenon in which aerodynamic forces and structural movement reinforce one another, causing increasingly severe oscillations.

The FAA has therefore determined that mandatory checks are necessary to ensure the affected components remain within acceptable limits.

Which Boeing 737 aircraft are affected?

The order covers specified aircraft from the Boeing 737 Next Generation family, rather than the newer 737 MAX series.

The affected models are the 737-600, 737-700, 737-700C, 737-800, 737-900 and 737-900ER. The directive applies to aircraft identified by the FAA’s referenced Boeing service information.

The FAA’s estimate of 1,987 aircraft relates to the US-registered fleet. It should not be interpreted as the total number of affected aircraft worldwide, said the FAA.

The directive follows an earlier proposal published in January. After reviewing feedback from airlines, Boeing and other stakeholders, the regulator finalised the requirements without relaxing the principal inspection deadlines.

What inspections must airlines carry out?

According to the directive, operators must measure freeplay in the left and right horizontal stabiliser pivot hinges and the jackscrew in accordance with Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-55A1104 RB, dated 12 June 2025.

Depending on the measurements and the aircraft’s condition, operators may need to carry out additional checks, repeat measurements at specified intervals, or repair or replace components that do not meet the required limits.

The FAA has rejected requests from some operators to extend certain inspection intervals, concluding that the prescribed schedule is necessary to maintain an acceptable level of safety.

However, the directive allows operators to seek approval for extensions if they can provide sufficient supporting data to demonstrate that the proposed alternative would maintain an acceptable level of safety.

The requirements also account for aircraft with replacement parts, meaning that installing new components does not automatically remove the need for subsequent inspections.

How much will the inspections cost?

The FAA estimates that the initial freeplay measurement will require approximately six labour hours per aircraft. Using an estimated labour rate of $85 per hour, the inspection is expected to cost around $510 per aircraft.

Across the estimated 1,987 affected US-registered aircraft, the initial inspection cost would total approximately $1.01 million.

These figures do not include the cost of repairs or replacement components where excessive freeplay is discovered. The final financial impact will therefore depend on the inspection findings and the work required by individual aircraft.

Will the order ground Boeing 737 aircraft?

No.

The directive does not impose a blanket grounding of the affected fleet. Instead, it establishes mandatory inspection and corrective-action requirements designed to identify excessive stabiliser movement before it develops into a more serious safety issue.

Airlines will need to incorporate the work into their maintenance programmes and comply with the specified deadlines.

Aircraft requiring repairs or replacement parts may need additional maintenance before they can continue operating, depending on the findings and applicable requirements.

The FAA’s decision highlights the importance of monitoring mechanical wear in flight-control systems, particularly where multiple operators have reported similar symptoms.

With the directive becoming effective on 23 November, affected operators will need to ensure their inspection plans meet the regulator’s requirements.

The order does not mean that all affected aircraft are unsafe to fly. Rather, it makes the checks legally mandatory to address a potential hazard and reduce the risk of a loss-of-control event.

]]> Supercomputer set to take AI to the Moon aboard Astrolab rover https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/supercomputer-ai-moon-aboard-astrolab-rover/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:48:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54243 Hewlett Packard Enterprise is preparing to send its Spaceborne Computer-4 to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s FLIP rover.

The post Supercomputer set to take AI to the Moon aboard Astrolab rover appeared first on AGN.

]]> A supercomputer capable of running artificial intelligence, including large language models, is preparing to travel to the Moon aboard a robotic rover later this year, in an experiment that could allow future lunar missions to analyse information and make decisions without constantly relying on controllers on Earth.

The Spaceborne Computer-4, developed by Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), is one of approximately 20 scientific and technology payloads aboard Astrolab’s 480 kg FLIP lunar rover, which is being prepared for launch as early as November. 

What will the FLIP lunar rover do on the Moon?

Alongside experiments involving artificial intelligence and advanced computing, the rover will carry instruments to map the lunar surface and investigate its composition.

The computer will attempt the first high-performance computing benchmarks on the lunar surface, alongside experiments involving AI-powered image analysis, navigation, document searches and cybersecurity.

The aim is to demonstrate that complex computing tasks normally performed in laboratories or data centres on Earth can be carried out directly on the Moon.

That capability could become increasingly important as NASA and commercial companies prepare for more frequent lunar missions, including operations in which robots must work for long periods without astronauts present.

HPE President and CEO Antonio Neri emphasised the importance of processing information directly on the Moon rather than relying entirely on computing facilities on Earth.

“As lunar activity accelerates, the ability to process data where it’s created will be critical to unlocking new scientific insights and supporting autonomous, sustained operations,” Neri wrote on LinkedIn.

He highlighted the company’s collaboration with NASA, the International Space Station National Laboratory, Astrolab, KIOXIA and Deloitte on the mission.

Scott Wiest, HPE’s vice president, fellow and global sales chief technologist said, “The next chapter of lunar exploration will depend on the ability to turn data into insights at the point of discovery.”

“With HPE Spaceborne Computer-4, we are bringing AI and high-performance computing to the lunar edge, helping the acceleration of scientific discovery and building the infrastructure for the next era of exploration,” Wiest added.

The mission is expected to launch in November 2026 under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. Its success, including the computer’s performance in the lunar environment, remains to be demonstrated.

Why take a supercomputer to the Moon?

Spacecraft traditionally collect information and transmit much of it to Earth, where engineers and scientists analyse the results and send instructions back.

That approach works, but communications take time and bandwidth is limited. The difficulty becomes greater as missions travel further from Earth.

A computer capable of processing images, identifying hazards and interpreting scientific observations directly aboard a rover could reduce the amount of information that must be transmitted.

This approach is known as edge computing: instead of sending everything to a distant data centre, information is processed close to where it is collected.

HPE’s system will combine a central processing unit, or CPU, with a graphics processing unit, or GPU. The CPU handles general computing tasks, while the GPU can perform many calculations simultaneously, making it useful for AI and image processing.

High-performance computing, or HPC, refers to using substantial computing power to solve complex problems. On FLIP, the objective is not to reproduce a large terrestrial supercomputer, but to test advanced computing workloads using a compact module designed for space.

The distinction is important. The planned lunar experiments will assess whether such technology can operate reliably under conditions that are very different from those on Earth.

AI that can read, analyse and navigate

Among the experiments planned for the mission are specialised large language models, or LLMs, the type of AI technology used in conversational systems.

On the Moon, their role will be different from answering everyday questions.

The models will be tested on tasks such as searching technical documents, interpreting information and helping researchers make sense of data collected by the rover.

HPE also plans to process images and measurements from LiDAR, a laser-based system that measures distances to surrounding objects and builds three-dimensional maps. Such information could help a rover recognise obstacles, understand the terrain and identify safer routes.

NASA will contribute two AI experiments. One, called Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization (FLUID), will demonstrate coordination between three AI models using data associated with Earth, the Moon and the International Space Station.

The other will test a specially adapted language model that can search and interpret documents stored aboard the spacecraft.

Deloitte will contribute Silent Shield, a system intended to identify unusual computer activity and potential cyber intrusions.

The experiments are demonstrations, not evidence that an AI system is ready to control future lunar missions independently.

Surviving the lunar environment

Running advanced computing equipment on the Moon presents difficulties that do not exist inside an ordinary data centre.

There is almost no atmosphere to carry away heat, temperatures vary enormously between sunlit and shaded areas, and electronics are exposed to radiation.

HPE has designed Spaceborne Computer-4 as a lightweight, self-contained unit without conventional cooling fans. It will use the rover’s thermal management system to help control its temperature.

The module includes low-power processors and solid-state storage supplied by KIOXIA. Unlike traditional hard drives, solid-state drives have no moving parts.

HPE is also using software to protect the computer against radiation-related disturbances.

As MIT Technology Review reported on 20 October, the company’s approach builds on earlier Spaceborne computers tested aboard the International Space Station. The software monitors the system for problems and can reduce processing speed and power when radiation conditions become hazardous.

HPE chief scientist and principal investigator Mark Fernandez explained the difficulty of operating equipment that cannot be repaired easily.

“In space, we don’t have the redundancy, we don’t have the repairman, we don’t have the spare parts,” he said, according to MIT Technology Review.

The company has previously flown three generations of Spaceborne computers to the ISS. The programme has demonstrated that commercially derived computing hardware can operate in space with appropriate protection.

In 2025, the ISS programme also tested Meta’s Llama 3.2 language model as part of the Space Llama initiative.

The Moon presents a tougher test because the equipment will operate outside the comparatively controlled environment of a crewed space station.

Astrolab’s rover and the Artemis connection

The computer will travel aboard FLIP, short for FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform, an approximately 480-kilogram robotic rover developed by California-based Venturi Astrolab.

FLIP is intended to carry around 20 scientific and technology payloads, including equipment for mapping the lunar surface and investigating the composition of lunar soil.

The rover uses specialised deformable wheels designed to maintain traction on uneven terrain.

It is scheduled to be delivered near the lunar south pole aboard the Griffin-1 lander, part of NASA’s CLPS programme, which purchases lunar delivery services from commercial companies.

Astrolab founder and chief executive Jaret Matthews said the rover would provide an opportunity to test technologies under actual lunar conditions.

“Our FLIP rover is designed to accommodate a variety of payloads, and this mission will demonstrate how commercial lunar mobility platforms can support technology development and scientific research.”

Astrolab also has a separate role in NASA’s Artemis lunar exploration programme.

In May 2026, NASA selected the company as one of two providers of crewed lunar rovers under its revised surface mobility plans.

The approximately $219 million task order covers development and delivery of the CLV-1 vehicle, which is intended to transport astronauts and equipment around the lunar south pole.

CLV-1 is a different vehicle from FLIP. It is designed to carry astronauts, while FLIP is an uncrewed technology and science platform.

The crewed rover draws on Astrolab’s FLEX architecture and technology developed with Venturi Space, including wheels, batteries and battery management systems.

NASA expects the newly contracted crewed vehicles to reach the Moon by 2028.

NASA is already using AI to study the Moon

The planned computing experiment comes as NASA expands the use of artificial intelligence in lunar research.

In September, NASA and IBM released a Lunar Foundation Model trained primarily on images collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The model was developed using roughly two million image tiles, including more than one million high-resolution camera images and nearly 964,000 multispectral images.

Researchers can adapt it to identify craters, investigate volcanic features and estimate where ice might remain stable near the lunar poles.

Kevin Murphy, NASA’s chief science data officer and acting chief data and AI officer, said the challenge was making decades of observations easier to use.

“We also have to make data easier for scientists to explore and use,” he said.

Unlike HPE’s proposed lunar experiment, the NASA-IBM model is designed for scientific analysis rather than specifically for operation aboard FLIP. Both developments, however, reflect growing interest in using AI to extract useful information from large quantities of space data.

From experiment to future lunar operations

The immediate objective for HPE is to establish that advanced computing can function reliably on the lunar surface.

Its planned tests include two established computing benchmarks, High Performance LINPACK and High Performance Conjugate Gradient, which measure different aspects of a computer’s ability to perform demanding calculations.

HPE will also support Astrolab’s mission control in Hawthorne, California, using its private cloud and operations software.

]]> F-117 Nighthawk: Restored legendary stealth aircraft joins the Smithsonian Collection https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/restored-lockheed-f117-smithsonian-collection/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54177 With its stealth capabilities, the selected aircraft has a remarkable operational record, having flown live missions in four major conflicts.

The post F-117 Nighthawk: Restored legendary stealth aircraft joins the Smithsonian Collection appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Lockheed F-117A Nighthawk, one of the most revolutionary military aircraft ever developed, is preparing to take its place among aviation history’s most significant machines at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum.

Nicknamed ‘The Overachiever’, the aircraft (serial number #818) has a remarkable operational record, having flown combat missions in all four major conflicts in which the F-117 participated.

The US Air Force (USAF) transferred the aircraft (serial number 818) to the museum in October 2026, following an announcement by Lockheed Martin and the Smithsonian in September.

After restoration and reassembly, it is expected to go on public display at the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Centre in Chantilly, Virginia, near Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

A unique aircraft with a remarkable history

The F-117A Nighthawk holds a special place in military aviation as the world’s first operational stealth combat aircraft.

Developed in secrecy by Lockheed’s celebrated Skunk Works division, it introduced a new approach to aerial warfare, allowing the USAF to attack heavily defended targets while greatly reducing the likelihood of detection by enemy radar.

Aircraft 818 joining the Smithsonian collection is particularly significant. Known as The Overachiever, it is the only F-117 documented as having flown combat missions in all four major conflicts involving the type – Operation Just Cause in Panama in 1989, Operation Desert Storm in Iraq in 1991, Operation Allied Force over Yugoslavia in 1999, and Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq in 2003.

Its service during the 1991 Gulf War helped establish the F-117’s legendary reputation. Nighthawks penetrated Iraqi airspace to strike strategically important targets, including command facilities and air-defence installations.

Their ability to approach targets with a reduced radar signature gave commanders an important new option at the opening of an air campaign.

According to US military reporting, the featured aircraft flew 1,271 sorties during its participation in the 1991 conflict, achieving an 80% mission success rate without sustaining battle damage.

What was the F-117 Nighthawk?

Despite its official F-117 designation, the Nighthawk was not a conventional fighter designed to engage enemy aircraft in air-to-air combat.

It was a specialised, single-seat attack aircraft developed primarily to penetrate defended airspace and destroy high-value ground targets.

Its development began during the 1970s, when the US military sought ways to counter increasingly capable radar-guided surface-to-air missile systems.

Lockheed’s Skunk Works developed an aircraft whose distinctive angular surfaces helped deflect radar waves away from their source. Radar-absorbent materials further reduced its visibility to enemy detection systems.

The result was an aircraft that looked unlike anything previously seen in operational military service. Its sharply faceted black exterior, unusual planform and carefully shaped surfaces were designed around stealth rather than conventional aerodynamic elegance.

The F-117 first flew in 1981 and achieved initial operational capability in 1983. Its existence remained classified for years, with the US government publicly acknowledging the programme in 1988. The aircraft made its first formal public appearance in 1990.

Although the F-117 was officially designated a fighter, its actual role was precision ground attack. It was used to destroy command-and-control facilities, air-defence systems and other strategically important targets, often operating at night to further reduce the risk of detection.

When was the F-117 retired?

The US Air Force officially retired the F-117 fleet in 2008, following more than two decades of service. Its pioneering capabilities had helped pave the way for newer stealth platforms, including the B-2 Spirit bomber and the F-22 Raptor.

The F-35 Lightning II also belongs to the wider generation of aircraft benefiting from advances in low-observable technology.

Retirement did not mean the immediate disappearance of every Nighthawk. Some aircraft remained in storage and selected examples continued to appear in training and test activities after the fleet’s formal withdrawal from operational service.

For The Overachiever, the move to the Smithsonian represents a new chapter. Before its transfer, Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works team prepared the aircraft for public exhibition, removing sensitive military equipment and making the necessary changes to preserve its appearance without exposing classified technology.

Its wings and fuselage were transported separately aboard a USAF C-5M Super Galaxy before being delivered to Virginia.

Preserving a milestone in aviation history

The National Air and Space Museum’s acquisition ensures that visitors will be able to examine one of the aircraft that transformed modern military aviation up close.

The Udvar-Hazy Centre, located near Washington Dulles International Airport, houses a substantial collection of historic aircraft and spacecraft. The Nighthawk’s arrival adds an important example of the technological changes that shaped air power at the end of the Cold War and beyond.

For aviation enthusiasts, The Overachiever is more than an unusually shaped aircraft. It represents the moment when stealth moved from an experimental concept to a practical combat capability, changing how military aircraft were designed and how air campaigns could be conducted.

Once hidden behind layers of secrecy, the F-117 will now be preserved for the public as a landmark in aerospace engineering. Its transition from frontline attack aircraft to museum exhibit provides a fitting tribute to a machine whose influence extends well beyond its years in active service.

]]> Airbus expects demand for 2,670 freighter aircraft over the next two decades, as airlines and cargo operators replace ageing aircraft and respond to growing demand for air freight.

Rather than purchasing a new aircraft, operators can give an existing passenger jet a second life by transforming its cabin into a cargo compartment.

This involves modifications including reinforced floors, cargo loading doors and systems designed to carry freight.

Airbus offers passenger-to-freighter conversion options across its A320, A321 and A330 families, providing operators with aircraft for different cargo needs.

The company said it had secured 34 orders for the aircraft this year and that certification activity with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) was progressing.

The A350F completed its maiden flight on 29 September, marking a key milestone for the programme. Airbus is aiming to strengthen its position in the large widebody freighter segment, a market long dominated by Boeing.

Designed to carry up to 111 tonnes of freight, the A350F has a range of 8,700km and features an electrically operated main-deck cargo door. At 4.3m wide, Airbus says it is the industry’s largest main-deck cargo door.

The aircraft is designed to accommodate standard containers and pallets, as well as oversized cargo including large aircraft engines.

According to Airbus, the A350F will deliver lower fuel burn and CO₂ emissions than previous-generation freighters.

North America and Asia-Pacific are expected to account for almost two-thirds of global demand, requiring 925 and 850 aircraft respectively.

Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) are forecast to require 515 aircraft, followed by Latin America (165), the Middle East (125) and Africa (90).

Airbus expects Asia-Pacific to remain the world’s largest international air freight market, with traffic between Asia-Pacific and North America forecast to be the fastest-growing major corridor, expanding by 3.8% annually.

What’s driving growth in air cargo demand?

The rise of online shopping, expanding global trade and demand for faster deliveries are expected to support growth in air cargo traffic over the next two decades. Freight aircraft play an important role in moving time-sensitive and high-value goods, from consumer electronics and pharmaceuticals to industrial equipment and aircraft parts.

Airbus believes this growth, combined with the retirement of older aircraft, will create demand for thousands of additional freighters.
